speechtext:
Three days ago I directed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He referred me to the Minister of Finance. My question was as follows:
Has the Canadian government recently made any representations to the government of the United States asking for a new trade treaty to reduce the tariffs between the two nations, this apart from the Geneva or the Havana agreements? If so, has the American government made any response?
National Housing Act

Now that the minister has returned from the United States, can he make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TARIFFS AND TRADE
subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES-QUESTION AS TO REDUCTION IN CUSTOMS DUTIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend's question was
brought to my attention, and I should like to reply as follows. Discussions are constantly taking place between the officials of the two countries on all phases of our economic relations with the United States, including, of course, our trade relations. However, the Canadian government have not made representations recently to the government of the United States for a new trade treaty to reduce tariffs. For reasons which must be well known to the hon. member, it is considered that circumstances in the United States at present are not propitious for specific tariff negotiations. I can assure the hon. member that as soon as the circumstances are more propitious the Canadian government will take the earliest opportunity to propose further negotiations for reductions in tariff barriers between the two countries.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the National Housing Act, 1944, and in particular to authorize approved lending institutions to purchase from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages held by the said corporation and to make loans to owners of rental housing projects not exceeding in amount 85 per cent of the estimated cost thereof; to authorize Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to guarantee an annual return of an amount to be determined by the corporation of rentals from rental housing projects for a period not exceeding thirty years, to make loans to owners of rental housing projects if such loans are not being made available by approved lend>-ing institutions; to authorize the governor in council to transfer lands vested in His Majesty to the corporation; and to make provision for the winding-up and dissolution of Wartime Housing Limited and to vest in Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation power to provide rental housing out of moneys which may be appropriated by parliament for the purpose.
Mr. J. 0. PROBE (Regina City): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply introduced his annual resolution on the subject of amendments to the National Housing Act, and made a statement as to activities in the past year and proposed government policy for the ensuing year. I wish to conclude the remarks I began yesterday by referring to the following points.

It is a matter of definite knowledge that the sharply increased construction costs which are hamstringing the building industry of this country, so far as home ownership and rental projects are concerned, are definitely tied up with the continuing decontrol policy of the government. As well as on the rental projects this has had a serious effect on persons who had small amounts of money saved up for the purpose of buying housing accommodation for their family needs. I want to emphasize that in view of the minister's continuing policy to protect vested capital and to ignore the needs of the home owner for protection, we are reaching the stage where these high construction costs will result in loss of investments to thousands of small and middle income owners who have managed to secure a small equity in property which they were forced to buy in order to find a place in which to live, and the high amortization costs with which they are undoubtedly faced in reducing their indebtedness will have the effect of wiping out their equity should there be any recession in the near future. In view of the fact that the government has seen fit to introduce with this resolution a further degree of protection for invested capital, I feel that the government should also work out a plan of equity insurance which would protect the investment of the home owner. The rental insurance clause which the minister referred to in his speech yesterday is of value only to the builder and the landlord in cases where there are eight or more family units. To indicate the extent to which the policy of the government with respect to past and present housing schemes has resulted in hardship, even where contracts have been signed, I want to give an example of what happens when costs rise to astronomical proportions as they are rising now in the building field.
I have here correspondence from a veteran who, to secure a home for his family, entered into what he thought was an ironclad contract with a construction company in the city of Regina, building under the integrated housing agreement last year, in 1947.
In his letter to me this veteran says:
An advertisement appeared in the Regina Leader-Post indicating that houses for veterans would be built at certain stated prices.
His statement in that regard is true, as my correspondence with Mr. Mansur, the president of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, indicates. Mr. Mansur in his letter to me stated that the original maximum sale price of the house I speak of was fixed at 86,050, although subsequently it turned out that this veteran

National Housing Act
had to pay $7,160 for it. Continuing from the letter of this veteran:
Under ordinary circumstances, I am sure I would have gone very carefully into the matter of contract and the provisions for its completion being secured at the price indicated. However, being a veteran, and inasmuch as the proposition apparently was to be guaranteed by the dominion government and financed by a reliable and reputable mortgage company, the precautions that ordinarily would be taken were not taken by myself. I felt, and I am sure that most of the other veterans felt that, regardless of their political belief, in view of the fact that the scheme was sponsored by the dominion government and was being handled by a mortgage company as indicated, ordinary precautions could be waived and that a reasonable degree of trust and confidence could be placed in a scheme that was so advertised and so sponsored. Apparently our confidence was entirely misplaced.
Here is the situation. The construction company, finding that the costs, which the company itself was incurring, were rising, had protected itself by having an escalator clause put in the contract with the unsuspecting veteran, the effect of which was that the veteran had to increase his payment beyond what he thought he would be paying, from $6,050 to $7,160. The point I make is this. The construction company is protected completely by funds of the people of Canada, but the man who has to pay the bill has no protection under our legislation or by the regulations of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. He was left to the caprice of changing conditions and the government's decontrol policy. Having caused these prices to rise, even after the contract was let for the construction of these houses, the government was morally obligated to meet that advancing cost.
The minister spoke of an improved supply situation and I must say, to be as kind to him as I can, that he is anything but realistic. Reference was made, yesterday and previously, to a subsidy to Crane Limited. Again, they are protected, but there is no protection for the buyer of plumbing to ensure that he will get fixtures at a reasonable cost. The minister spoke of arrangements with the steel companies to produce nails, but builders still have not sufficient nails. In my city of Regina no one is able to make sure of a supply of nails. The export of the best timber from this country continues, with no guarantee of fair prices to the domestic user. Rising freight rates of 21 per cent, authorized by the cabinet, have had the effect of adding from seven per cent to ten per cent to the cost of houses which are currently going up. It has been mentioned in this house that building labour is high in cost and also inefficient. May I tell the house that when workmen are on a job and there are certain materials in short supply, and when
you get dribs and drabs of those materials, you cannot expect labour to be anything but wasteful of time and inefficient in the use of that time, and through no fault of their own.
The whole emphasis in the government's program, except for wartime housing, is the protection of the investment company, and I say that, even here, public housing authorities of a community nature, municipal or co-operative, are not given equal consideration with private enterprise when it comes to guarantees of equity such as are normally given by legislation to investment companies.
The minister said yesterday that the proposals of the Canadian federation of mayors regarding the low-rental portion of their program on housing had merit, and then he went on to say that they were not acceptable in their present form chiefly because they contemplate full financing by the dominion government, both in respect of capital costs and in respect of operating deficits. Now the government is willing to guarantee the operating deficits and profits of investment companies but is not willing to give the same consideration to public housing authorities.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What do they undertake to do in return?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
They undertake simply to build houses, and as a matter of fact they did not build them. They went out of the picture and the government is guaranteeing them full costs with a fair return on their investment.
I suggest to the minister in conclusion that he put building products once more under price control, set all necessary export embargoes, through the cabinet of course, and go into the production business on short items if necessary, either in his own capacity or by way of crown corporations.
The second thing, which unhappily he is unable to get through that skull of his, is this. He will not resign himself to the absolute necessity of capital subsidies to low-rental projects, a thing that has been recognized for half a century in practically all countries which are interested in social wellbeing; and in addition to resigning himself to the need for capital subsidies for low-rental projects, he should make arrangements through public authorities who are interested in the economies that may
National Housing Act

be secured rather than through private investment companies who get cost plus at every stage.
Further, I suggest that he expand rather than diminish the activities of Wartime Housing, which apparently, by the terms of this bill, are to be taken over by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Wartime Housing has done a useful job and comes closest to providing housing at a rental that low-income families can pay. In the minister's statement to the house yesterday we see that the activities of Wartime Housing are to be restricted.
I suggest further that the minister set up a special branch of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build or to buy houses for veteran owners who may wish them in urban or rural areas, the Department of Veterans Affairs to be asked to contribute as they are now doing with regard to small holdings. The small holding feature is an excellent thing, but there are too many veterans who cannot take advantage of it because of one restriction or another, or because they find that the project is not suitable. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation therefore should make a special effort to meet the needs of veteran housing in whatever districts the veterans want their houses placed.
A high priority should be given to the rental accommodation needs of families now occupying homes which were bought a year or more ago for bona fide occupation by purchasers with families. It seems to me that they are entitled to the enjoyment and use of the house they bought for themselves, and it is up to the minister's department to find alternative occupation for those who, as a result of government policy, are kept in possession, while other people who have the same need are kept out.
Finally, it seems to me it is time the minister studied and applied the lesson that other countries have learned, namely, that private enterprise cannot build low-rental housing, because of the nature of our competitive economy. Whether the government consider themselves as socialists or capitalists, they must learn, as other countries have, that public housing for low-income families is the only solution to the problem and the only method of achieving the objective of a decently housed Canadian people.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the things we can remember quite well is that during the war everybody in Canada was told that when those who were in uniform came back from the war they

would have a Canada worth living in, and that everybody would have a house in which to live. Not only was that stated, but emphasis was given to the prophecy that costs would be coming down in view of the fact that our productive ability had so greatly increased. It was argued that that fact of itself would bring prices down. We find that is not quite so, particularly in the field of housing.
In his speech the other day the minister went to great lengths to show the need for housing. I am not so sure that it was necessary for him to go to such length to prove that point, because everyone is aware of it. It will be noticed that the minister made the following statement as reported at page 3639 of Hansard-and I commend him for having done so:
In spite of the resulting higher sale prices, the effective demand for home ownership continues. The number of completed but unsold houses is relatively small. For instance, in the city of Vancouver, where proportionately there is more new housing than in any other place in the dominion, completed but unsold houses amount to less than one week's supply of new houses. The same situation pertains generally throughout the country.
I think that is an accurate picture, that there is not even one week's supply of new houses in excess of demand.

speechtext:
I think the building concerns across Canada have the ability to cope with this problem. Private enterprise could cope with it if a little encouragement were given to them, despite what the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) has said-and I shall refer to that in a moment.
The minister pointed out that these houses were in greater demand, but he pointed out further, and rightly so, that the type of house

National Housing Act
which is in greater demand now is the rental house. The reason is obvious. Under the present increasing prices; the ordinary person cannot afford to build; the only recourse he has, therefore, is to rent. The situation is now becoming so acute that even those who desire to rent a house cannot do so, because of their limited financial position.
The minister spoke about the cost of houses, and he said, if I recall it correctly, that a five-room house could be built for about $6,800 and would rent at $37.50. That might be true if Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are building the houses, or if Housing Enterprises Limited are building them. But I do not think it is true if a private person is trying to build a house for rent. Certainly the private individual cannot build a five-room house, on his own behalf, for $6,800.
About two weeks ago I had occasion to assist a veteran to get some property under the Veterans Land Act on which to build a house. This man is complying with all the regulations, and is building a four-room house, without lath or plaster. It is costing him over $6,000. If you intend to build a five-room house and have it lathed and plastered, which I think it should be, I do not think you can do it for another $500 or $600. It is becoming particularly difficult now for the private individual to finance his own house.' The minister in his speech said that every encouragement should be given to individuals to build their own houses. I agree with that idea one hundred per cent. But unless there is some other means of assisting them to do so, I do not think they will be able to build them. I mentioned a moment ago that some of the large corporations, such as Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, may be able to do that. When building is being done on a large scale, and when there is access to all the materials, and where there is no shortage coming in to cause a holdup, houses may be built; but the individual builder is not in that position, because of the scarcity of materials.
The minister went on to point out that there was an adequate supply of most materials. If I remember correctly the minister said there was a fair supply of lumber; and he even went so far as to say there was a fair supply of nails. That is not so in the west. It is true that there is an ample supply of rough construction material for studding, roofing and things of that kind, for roughing-in the building. but certainly there is a lack of finished material. There is a definite shortage of plumbing and of soil pipe, and there is a terrific shortage of nails. That question is so important it was mentioned the other day in
the prices committee, to see if something could not be done to alleviate the great distress that is occasioned through this nail shortage.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
There is another point I want to emphasize along the line of the hon. gentleman's interjection. There does not seem to be any shortage of nails as far as these large contractors are concerned, particularly Central Mortgage and Housing and Building Enterprises; but when it comes to the ordinary man he just cannot get nails. That situation has not been remedied in the last six months or so, either. When I was home at Easter, contractors came to me asking what was the matter with the supply of nails. I had to tell them I did not see how there could be a shortage, because the minister of reconstruction said there were plenty of them. I will not attempt to put on Hansard what they called the minister, because I am sure the Speaker would say it was out of order. It might be appropriate, but still it would be out of order.
In his speech the minister said these $6,800 five-room houses could be rented for $37.50. That may be true, as far as Central Mortgage and Housing is concerned, or Wartime Housing, but I do not know of a single $7,000 house that can be rented for $37.50. They just do not exist except under those two corporations; and there are so many people within the low income brackets who cannot afford $37.50 and in addition supply heat, light and water. I do not see how we are going to have low rental housing, Mr. Speaker, other than by subsidization. Certainly under present conditions it cannot be done. In his speech even the minister pointed out that they were going out of house building because of increased costs. But it makes no difference whether costs are increasing, as they are for one reason and another; people must have places in which to live, and you cannot just say you are going to wash your hands of the whole problem because of increased costs.
The minister went on to point out emphatically that they could not continue in this field unless they could build a five-room house which would rent for a nominal amount such as $37.50. I can see the point, because taking the increased cost factor into consideration they would go behind. But I suggest that it is much better for the government to go behind than for the individual, who has not the money; and believe me, there are plenty of people in this country, including returned soldiers, earning only $35 a week. The person
National Housing Act

to whom I was referring a short time ago is a returned soldier with a family, living on $35 a week. Can anyone tell me how he is going to be able to pay even $37.50 for a house, then heat it and pay for the light and water, and in addition take care of his family? How are you going to meet a situation such as that unless you do subsidize housing?
I want to mention a matter which I have not discussed with the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply but which I have taken up with the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who I must say was very considerate and took action to remedy the situation. I have in mind the speculation that is going on in these wartime and veterans' houses. I have had some experience with that of late. There are instances- how many I do not know-such as this. A veteran of the first war, who is in an excellent financial position, with a good job, because of his priority, has held land under the Veterans Land Act for as long as two and three years, while other veterans right in the same locality cannot get land on which to build the houses they so greatly need. I do not think this act and the Veterans Land Act were ever intended to be used for speculation, though in fairness I must say that when I brought the matter to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs he acted immediately and the particular difficulty was solved. I have other cases I am going to bring to his attention as well, and I am sure they will receive the same consideration. But I want to tell the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply that in the city of Calgary there are men living in wartime houses who own one or two other houses in the same city. I do not think that is right. I often wonder how many men who have these veterans' holdings or wartime houses, for which they pay a nominal rental of perhaps $22.50 per month, at the same time have property in their own name which they are renting for anywhere from $50 to $75 a month, and probably some property in the names of their wives which is being rented for a similar amount. I believe that is something the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply should look into a little more fully. If that situation exists in one city I am sure it must exist in others, and I believe there should be a thorough investigation right across Canada.
I must say that I have come across these cases by accident. The first inkling I had of this situation was in connection with the Veterans Land Act, the matter I said had been cleared up by the minister. I want to bring it to the attention of the minister of reconstruction, however, so that he may look into the whole problem. When he went to the
fMr. Johnston.]
Veterans Land Act administration there was not a piece of land in Calgary that had not been taken; that is what I was told by the officials. After a little discussion, however, we found that there were seven or eight veterans who had priority claims on these lots and who had not done anything about them for a long time. The officials were going to take the matter into consideration, and when I asked how long they would require to consider it they mentioned three or four months. When I came to Ottawa and discussed it with the minister, however, it was only a matter of days until the matter was settled. Here were veterans, not only one but dozens, trying to get property on which to build and being held up because other veterans were holding the land for speculation; and as I have indicated, the same thing is going on under wartime housing, where men who have good positions and who have city property of their own, are living in these wartime houses at low rentals.
I do not want to say any more than I have said on this question, Mr. Speaker, but when we get into committee I think of necessity it will have to be gone into in greater detail.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says it is a boner; we shall see why.
One of the first things done by the minister about housing was in connection with a system of building priorities. I do not intend to go into that in any detail. It was a means of regulating and channelling building materials into the hands of those who were conducting building projects approved or sponsored by the government. This process of priority worked, up to a point. It did stifle private builders to a very great extent, but it also provided the kind of housing the government was sponsoring. That, however, has now reached the point where there are only one or two building items actually affected by priorities.
We come now to the matter of integrated housing. As hon. members know, integrated housing is a means whereby certain builders agree to build houses and to obtain in respect of them certain limited profits as set by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. At the same time they get priorities in building materials. That system has worked, to a point; but there could not be enough builders, and there have not been enough builders interested in the project to the extent of making it national in scope.
I hold in my hand a return I received in 1947. Up to May 14 of that year only 1,691 housing units had been started under agreement. The number last year was not extensive. Although a great many first-class builders have taken part in this project, it does not begin to solve our housing problem in Canada.
Last year the minister brought in another expedient by way of amendment to the National Housing Act under which approved lending corporations and insurance companies were allowed to enter the field of developing land in order that housing projects might be built on that land. As we know, the subdividing of land and its servicing with water, sewer and sidewalk facilities, and the making of provision to see that they are close to schools, and the like, is an expensive business.
National Housing Act

This was an important step forward. May I say, however, that I received a return in February last from the Department of Trade and Commerce in which I had asked how many of these subdivision projects had been started. The reply was that there were only six throughout the whole of Canada, two of which were in Ontario, one at Burlington and one in North York, adjoining Toronto. I am not competent to speak for all of these projects, but upon investigation I found that in connection with the one in North York the lots were being sold for from $2,250 to $2,400 each. That was not my understanding of the purpose of the project, nor was it my idea of the work the project was to do. I was under the impression that this was something to help the builder to go ahead with low-cost housing, which would be suitable for the average citizen, on lots at perhaps $600 or $800. But when the cost of the lot gets up to $2,250 or $2,400, in my opinion no purpose is being served by the plan.
I am disappointed in that plan, which I commended the minister for adopting. He is our leader in matters of housing, and if he cannot do the job himself, somebody in his department should take over this thing and make it work. It is most important that land be provided in cities or closely adjacent thereto for housing purposes. The minister himself has said on more than one occasion that lack of land was one of the big obstacles. We have the lending institutions and the big insurance companies with ability to make this very project a success, but it is making no progress at all. That is the kind of building program which we thought would serve a useful purpose, but it has not, and we are forced to the conclusion that these expedients must give place to an efficient building program.
Next came Housing Enterprises Limited which was going to take its share of responsibility for providing rental housing units. But what happened? They folded up in about a year and a half and disposed of all their assets to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. They found they could not compete economically with the class of houses being built by private enterprise. As a matter of fact their costs ran so high in overhead and accessories that they could not provide economic rental housing. Recognizing its futility, the department ended that project. It was a temporary expedient which has gone the way of a lot of others of its kind. Housing Enterprises Limited is no longer in existence.
[Hr. Timmins.]
Last year another attempt was made to do something about rental housing. The minister, by P.C. 1095 of March 25, 1945, provided for double depreciation to builders in respect of rental housing projects. That was an attempt on the part of the department to induce builders to go into the business of providing rental housing, but I understand that application for double depreciation has been made in the case of only 370 units. As a matter of fact provision is made for building up to January 1, 1949, only. I presume that any rental housing project started after that date is out. But it makes no difference whether it goes beyond January 1, 1949, or not, because it is just another temporary expedient in this game of trial and error which has been found wanting; it has not succeeded.
Wartime Housing is one of the crown companies which has succeeded up to a point. The minister has used it to provide rental housing for veterans, and it has succeeded in providing that kind of housing. Wartime Housing, however, is to be wound up under this resolution, and I presume that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will take its place. I do hope that this does not mean that the question of housing is to be handled now at the administrative level by a crown company instead of at the executive level. Perhaps the minister will explain just what the position is to be, because we as members of parliament cannot afford to have housing in Canada dealt with at the administrative level. It must be dealt with at the executive level.
I come now to the new feature in this resolution which the minister has called rental insurance. It is an involved proposal, by which apparently the builder is left in a secondary position, because the minister says, at page 3641 of Hansard:
The proposal before the house is designed to make rental housing more attractive to professional landlords and investors.
I do not believe that the average builder will be able to fit himself into the minister's plan in respect to rental housing. First of all, the minimum requirement is that the project shall consist of eight or more family housing units. That is not a project into which the average builder can go. He might build one or two units, but not the minimum of eight or more. He would not have sufficient capital to build more than one or two of these family housing units before his money would be tied up. It would be fatal to Canada if the small builder went into a project such as this and found that he had tied up all his money and

National Housing Act
had to sit down and wait for thirty years, which is the life of this project, for it to develop. I do not believe there is any place in this rental insurance plan for the private builder, and if there is no place in it for him, what class of citizen will be interested in it? The minister says, professional landlords and investors. I have had twenty-five years' experience in house management, and having regard to this rigorous climate of ours, I do not believe many people will be interested in building under this plan, hoping over a period of years to make a profit out of the venture. I think it is a step in the dark. The minister himself says that he is not so sure it is going to succeed. He says at page 3642 of Hansard:
We are not sure of the amount of new rental housing which will result from this proposal. We hope it will be substantial, and every effort will be made to encourage builders to operate under its provisions. It is likely, however, that most of the new housing will be in the moderate rental field because that is the type of housing in which landlords and builders are interested.
My own feeling is that it is not likely to succeed. It is another temporary expedient in the game of trial and error, and the only new matter which the government is bringing forward in respect to housing in 1948. I do not think it is sufficient. Cycles occur when unorthodox methods which were never before used have to be adopted. Great Britain in 1920 had to provide housing, whether they liked it or not, and they started a housing plan at that time. We in Canada are faced with the same problem today, and I want to emphasize some of the factors that are known to every one of us.
First of ail there is overcrowding. Our people are living together under conditions which are not healthy, and are sometimes unsanitary, and as a result there has been and continues to be a breakdown in the moral fibre of our people living under those conditions. I am sure that every member of the house knows something of the vicious consequences to our family life that come from people being forced to live together under conditions that are not proper. A short time ago we read in the papers of a shooting in the province of Quebec. I can myself remember at least three or four cases which have been brought up in the police court because of differences of opinion, fights and brawls, which have occurred between landlord and tenant, in which the landlord was asserting everything within the law and outside the law in order to get his tenant out. People are living in physical fear of assault, and assaults are taking place. That is one of the conditions for which we as members of parliament have to take some responsibility.
The second matter I want to mention is emergency housing. The minister was good enough to say that in his opinion we were over the peak in the matter of emergency housing. That may be so. However, people are being shifted into emergency housing in the city from which I come, every day in the week. I have had occasion recently to deal with people who felt that the municipality was responsible for them, for their housing and for their future maintenance. I have had them say to me, "I wish you would put the bailiff in here, because I cannot do this and that; I cannot get any housing accommodation until the sheriff comes in and puts me out. The welfare department will not do anything about it until the sheriff actually comes in and starts to move my stuff." These people have lost all sense of responsibility; they are just shifting about, and are being placed hither and thither by the welfare department. They have become charges upon the city because of the present housing situation. It is a state of mind that they have got themselves into.
Then, of course, there is another serious side to it. A sort of race suicide has developed. Young couples are getting married but they cannot have children for the simple reason that they have no place in which to put them. This is not a joke; it is a fact. The National Housing Act people have been working on this act for seven or eight years. They have got the thing down to the point where they seem to fix their attention upon a small house for the parents and two children. It has to be two boys or two girls. There is no room for a boy and a girl because there are just two bedrooms. If you look at the plans you will see that there is no provision for extensions or additions to the house. I have seen some of the worst looking messes made of houses because the occupant tried to make an addition to it to provide for his growing family. It is a serious matter that those who are planning our future in this country so far as housing is concerned are not looking further ahead on this, but are constructing houses for a man, his wife and two children. If that is not race suicide, I do not know what it is. Fifty thousand houses have been put up under that plan, and nobody seems to take it into account. I say now that that is one more reason why this government has to dc something about the matter of housing.
I come now to immigration. This is one place where we can all get together. The provinces and the federal government can get together on immigration. As we know, the Ontario government has brought out more

National Housing Act
than seven thousand people, and they are all settled. They have found places for themselves, but when they squeezed in, somebody else had to squeeze out. There is no question about that. Alberta has a plan on hand. They are not only bringing immigrants to the province but they are bringing out industry as well. Saskatchewan has a plan, and the federal government say that they have a plan to bring in some 20,000 immigrants by next June. Where will these people go? Is it any responsibility of the provinces? Is it any responsibility of the municipality? Is it any responsibility of the federal government? I say it is a joint responsibility, but for the most part the responsibility rests right here on the department which is responsible for these people coming to this country.
If the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not now handling the Department of Mines and Resources, which has to do with immigration, then there must be co-ordination within the executive council so that the problem can be solved.
We are not going through a passing phase in this matter of housing. We are in a national emergency. We must have these immigrants in Canada. The Prime Minister himself said that we cannot hope to hold this country with a population of twelve and a half million people. We appreciate that a large number of our problems, such as freight rates, can be solved if we have the population here. We know perfectly well that we are getting into a horrible economic position in the matter of trade abroad, and that if we do not have the people here to consume our own domestic products we may have economic chaos before we are through; therefore we must admit that we must have immigration. If we are to have immigration, then we must have housing, and now is the time to provide it.
At page 3642 of Hansard the minister said:
However, the dominion does not take a dogmatic stand in this matter, and we are willing to discuss with the provinces and municipalities a course of action which would lay a sound foundation for a long term national housing program. The Canadian federation of mayors has already sent us a brief concerning low-rental housing.
As I remember it, the mayors met here some time last year, I think it was in June. I received a copy of the brief that they sent in. They sent a brief in February of this year as well. If the minister is serious about this business of a conference and willingness to taka a share in a long term national housing plan, why does he not call a meeting of the municipalities and provinces so that the matter

can be dealt with? The Ontario government brought in a housing plan in 1948. Some of the features of it are to provide for the reduction of down payments on newly-built houses. It is a plan to fit in with the provisions of the National Housing Act, to make it easier for those who have not sufficient money to get part of the down payment in order that they may have houses. It is an attempt on the part of the Ontario government to co-ordinate its efforts with those of the federal government, and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply was good enough to say that it was a helpful measure. In addition to that, they say they hope to participate wTith the municipalities in financing a redevelopment where there appears to be a sound policy. This is another matter which engages the attention of the federal government. The Ontario government has provided funds so that projects may be handled at all levels of government.
Another feature of the Ontario act is that they say they wish to participate with municipalities that desire to take advantage of the federal low-rental housing plan. Some $30,000,000 has been set aside so that progress may be made in housing in Ontario. But Ontario is not alone in that respect. A similar act, containing different features, has been passed in Quebec under which the province provided for the sale of lots at one dollar to citizens intending to build private dwellings, and guaranteed them tax concessions for a twenty-five year period in order to assist them to obtain houses.
I suggest to the minister that if he is serious about paying some attention to the brief of the federation of mayors, and to the desire of the various provinces to see their problems solved, in so far as the provinces have a responsibility, now is the time to call a conference. After all, there is an election coming on in Ontario and there will be one in Quebec this year. Saskatchewan will have an election, and there may be one in Alberta. This is a good time to get the ministers together.

speechtext:
The minister is just putting off again; he has another temporary expedient there. He is going to deal with the new governments. I say to him in all kindness that I hope to put him on the spot this afternoon. I think we have been temporizing with the thing long enough. Let me say this to him without any rancour at all. The minister may

National Housing Act
object when we say it, but the fact is, that he has too many jobs. He does a good job with anything he tackles, but he cannot do a good job when he undertakes too many. I suggest to him that he hand over to someone else these powers he has under the National Housing Act.
A few years ago the minister was putting a lot of efficiency and drive into housing, but I think he is starting to slow down, and the business of import controls from the United States is now taking up his attention. Rightly so. I suggest therefore that unless he is serious about this proposal of his to discuss with the provinces and the municipalities a course of action which would lay a sound foundation for a long-term national housing program, he had better move over in the bed and let some other minister start this, because in all seriousness I feel that this is our No. 1 problem in Canada.
We have the various provinces in a cooperative mood. The minister can be quite persuasive wrhen he wishes to bring any matter to a head, and I think that in matters of public housing, in the promotion of these limited dividend corporations, in matters of slum clearance, this is the time to get started. We should make a start on them now.
If you look at all this legislation on housing you will find a guarantee running through them all. There is a guarantee under the National Housing Act, a guarantee under the insurance rental project, a guarantee all the way through. We are like the ostrich, sticking our head in the sand-at least the department is-and saying that we may never have to pay these things. The fact of the matter is that the government, we the people, will have to pay them some day.
Since we have a surplus of $800 million estimated for this year, let us make a start and deal with the matter in a businesslike way. Let us start on some of these projects. I do not put very much confidence in what the minister said yesterday, that we cannot proceed with these matters because building costs are too high. The member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) who has just sat down, suggested that was not a factor. Who knows whether building costs will come down, or when? After all, housing is not something that can be put off. If we need a roof over our head we need it now, not after building costs have come down.
I suggest to the minister that this is the time when these things must be brought to a head. What we need right now is leadership. We have co-operation, plenty of co-operation all across Canada. We have the co-operation
of the people, the co-operation of the municipalities. In Toronto last year one of the controllers, a Liberal on the city council, Mr. Balfour, announced to the press that in only a matter of a few days there would be a conference with respect to these matters. He seemed to be confident even in those days that a conference would be called and that this question of housing would be dealt with at the three levels of government.
Leadership rests with the government, and the people will not be satisfied until it is exercised-not in 1949, not after we find out whether the rental insurance plan will work, but now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on the resolution for two reasons. First, I represent a constituency where 75 per cent of the population live in urban centres, such as Shawinigan, Grand'Mere, La Tuque, and Almaville. Second, I wish to repeat in the house the warning sounded in the province of Quebec by both Protestant and Catholic religious authorities, in connection with the housing problem.
Yesterday, the right hon. the minister of reconstruction (Mr. Howe) said that 77,000 housing units had been built in 1947. In my opinion, last year's building program is inadequate to provide the minimum number of houses required to prevent the housing shortage from increasing, and it is barely half sufficient for normal needs. In 1944, the government appointed an advisory committee to inquire into the housing situation; the said committee submitted what is known as the Curtis report. According to that report, Canada should have built 77,700 dwellings per year for a period of ten years. It is easy to understand that the above is a minimum figure, but it is inadequate. Here is what the report says in that connection: (Text):
The figures reproduced in the present summary are those made on a minimum and restricted basis. In general, throughout the report, when alternative assumptions present themselves the lower one has been adopted. (Translation):
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the 77,700 housing units required to prevent the situation from growing worse represent but a minimum figure. It is inadequate for the following reasons: first, it tends only to the needs of city dwellers, who make up no more than 60 per cent of the population, and ignores the require-

National Housing Act
meats of the farming classes who are none the less of some importance. Second, this figure does not include childless couples. It deals only with families and not with those homemakers whom statisticians call:	"Household
non family". Yet, hundreds of thousands of requests for housing accommodation come from these people. Finally, it provides for the replacement of only 1 per cent of homes in need of repair or falling apart; houses are seemingly supposed to last one hundred years. However, two sources of information which differ substantially from the Curtis report, are, to my mind far more accurate: during its February convention of 1943, the Toronto Architects' Association showed that at the present time Canada needs from 110,000 to 150,000 houses per year. Another publication, The Letter Review of March 31, 1947 stated:
(Text):
It is entirely reasonable to argue from that single fact that, in present circumstances, anything less than 150,000 houses a year is wholly inadequate.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, what the government has accomplished during 1947 is barely half of what is required to solve the housing problem. What are the underlying causes of our difficulties in solving the housing problem? Shortage of labour was mentioned and it has also been said that the primary cause of the lack of progress in the building of houses could be ascribed to the paralysing effect of the strikes on production. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that labour does not account for the complete and total failure of the government in the building field. The causes are as follows: In 1941,
500,000	of our men were in the forces with roughly the same number employed in munition plants, producing shells and other war materials. At that time, construction in our country reached a total of $640,000,000. In 1942, our forces numbered 625,000 men and probably the same number were engaged in production of munitions and in other war duties. Nevertheless, construction reached a total of $635,000,000. In 1945, during the demobilization period, construction reached only $409,000,000. In 1946, when I assume that demobilization had been completed, and production of munitions and war equipment had ceased, construction amounted to only $450,000,000. Another reason which prevents me from accepting labour shortage as a reason for
the difficulties in which we find ourselves in regard to housing is that we pay more unemployment benefits than ever before. The Labour Gazette of February, 1947, indicates that there were 488,667 applications for unemployment insurance benefits in 1946. Any builder, prospective home-owner or supplier of building materials will tell you that it is not so much the shortage of man-power that is the cause of delays, but the shortage of building materials. Among these we might mention nails; electrical appliances, plumbing supplies and ready-to-use lumber of good quality. It might be well to ask where these supplies have gone, while the necessity for them at home is still so pressing as to create an extremely serious situation which has been forcibly called to our attention by all our sociologists. We need only to examine our exports of building materials or of materials needed for the production of same. The following figures are taken from the Canada Year Book for the years 1943-1944, and 1946, pages 491 to 553.
Exports

While there is a greater need than ever for building materials on the home market, exports are still being made. Two reasons are given for this.
The first is the fact that our economy requires exports to maintain a high level of employment.
I respectfully suggest that our present export trade is made up of temporary exports which cannot help to stabilize our economy in any way. Besides here is what the dominion statistician says about our export trade:
(Text):
Actually about 75 to 80 per cent of Canada's enormous export business since 1940 belongs in the category of temporary, abnormal, wartime trade, with only about 20 to 25 per cent in the category of normal and permanent trade.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, how can we expect to stabilize our economy by means of a type of export trade which statisticians themselves hold to be of au essentially temporary nature? I suggest that the exports which we are making at this time, and especially those which are meant for the United Kingdom, have absolutely no stabilizing effect on our economy, but serve

National Housing Act
only to favour Great Britain in such a way that she will eventually become the most dangerous competitor on world markets.
The second reason: Pity and sentiment. We are told that the people of Europe have suffered great difficulties, that they are in dire straits and that we must help them. I respectfully submit-even though in doing so I might offend some people-that the housing situation in Great Britain is less critical than in Canada.
I say, in the first place, that the situation is less serious in Great Britain, for the following reasons; first, from 1939 to 1945, the population of Britain decreased by about 600,000 while the population of Canada increased by nearly 800,000; second, throughout the war, huge numbers of troops were quartered in the United Kingdom and when they left, their shelters could lessen the seriousness of the housing problem; third, from 1930 to 1940, the almost complete efforts of the British nation were devoted to the building of houses.
Here is what I find on page 33 of the Curtis report:
(Text):
While at the beginning of the thirities residential construction was drastically curtailed in the United States and Canada, more houses were built in England aud Wales than ever before. In 1934 about 267,000 housing units were built in England and Wales or about 28,000 more than were built during the peak year of the twenties. Since 1934 the volume of residential construction in that country has increased steadily, only to be interrupted with the outbreak of the war in 1939.
(Translation):
Therefore, the situation is less serious in Great Britain than in Canada, and we are sacrificing the interests of the Canadian people in order to save, once again, the British people. Besides, the rumours which depict the entire population of Europe as suffering hardships are not all concordant. As a matter of fact, I have here an item from La Nouvelliste quoting a Canadian Press dispatch dated March 11, 1947, in which Lord Inverchapel is reported as having stated, at a banquet of the New York law school graduates:
The British envoy enumerated the factors which prove that Great Britain is not prostrate. At the end of 1946, she was exporting from 110 to 115 per cent more than in 1938. She is building houses at the rate of 250,000 a year.
I shall now read what the Gazette said on May 5, 1948, in quoting a dispatch sent from London by Ernest Chisholm Thomson:
(Text):
. . . Britain's first target of 750.000 "units of accommodation" will be achieved by the end
of the year ... in spite of adversities and vicissitudes. Britain was putting up more houses than any other country.
(Translation):
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that our export trade policy is a primary cause of our housing difficulties.
For the past year, ever since the matter was bungled, attempts have been made to place the burden of the housing problem upon provincial and municipal authorities. In theory, Mr. Speaker, I agree that the housing problem should be the responsibility of provincial or municipal authorities. But how can the provincial authorities be expected to do an adequate job when the federal government, through its export trade policy, is creating a disastrous condition with respect to building materials at home? Furthermore, how can the provincial governments be expected to carry out a satisfactory housing scheme when they are deprived of their main source of revenues by the federal government?
Mr. Speaker, to stress the importance of the housing problem, may I recall that the first Labour-Progressive member to appear in the house was elected in Cartier during 1945 or 1946, after taking advantage of the housing situation before his electors?
Every now and then I receive resolutions from all sorts of associations begging me to show more sympathy for Great Britain. Mr. Speaker, in 1945 I was elected under the banner of nationalism, and I challenge anyone to state that he has ever heard me say an unkind word about Great Britain. However, I believe that my first duty as member for St. Maurice-Lafleche is to work not in the interest of a foreign country-however much sympathy I may feel for that country-but to work for the Canadian people. And if it so happens that other countries suffer indirectly by it, or share less in our liberalities, I cannot do anything about it, I feel that my duty is to the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was last home about two weeks ago a family I have known for quite a few years asked me to call and see them. I found them living on the second floor of a small home on a street not far from where I live. This man and woman are getting on in years and are doubtless just an example of a multitude of others living under similar conditions. Their living room, dining room and kitchen was the same room, and I am sure it was not twelve feet square. They had a small bedroom adjoining, and they used the same toilet and bath as the other occupants of the house. I have known this gentleman for quite a few years. He worked for quite a long time for the Farmers' Dairy in Toronto and never at any time had a wage of any consequence. He was always subject to being laid off and, to my knowledge, was laid off on numerous occasions, and so he never had a chance to earn a competence with which to provide a home of his own. On the occasion of my visit he told me that he did not expect to live very long, that he could not endure the conditions under which he was living. As a matter of fact, he died two days ago. All I wish to say in connection with this matter is that doubtless thousands of men and women throughout Canada have gone to their graves through the inadequacy of the housing accommodation in Canada. I know of so many cases like the one I have just mentioned.
I had a good deal to do with building in my day and was more or less conversant with the whole building problem. I know the minister himself knows a great deal about building. I doubt whether any member of the House of Commons has had as much actual experience in building of one kind and another as the minister himself, and when he was appointed to take charge of housing I for one looked forward to his doing a big job. Why he has not been able to do it I do not know. I should like him to tell us whether he was obstructed in any way in carrying out what he was charged to do and certainly had the capacity to do. There must have been some reason.

When he took charge of housing I thought he would initiate some program of prefabricated housing. Maybe it could not be done under his department; I do not know. It has, however, been done in Great Britain and in France, and perhaps elsewhere, but I do know that it has been done in both those countries. Many of the prefabricated houses which have been erected in France were put together in Canada. For quite some time there was a very nice confortable prefabricated house on one of the main docks in Quebec city. I forget the name of the dock but I am sure the minister knows all about it. That prefabricated house was a model of what was being shipped to France. Speaking from memory, I think approximately 1,500 to 2,000 of these prefabricated houses have been shipped from Canada to France. The minister nods his head; I am glad to know that. It was a frame house, neatly constructed, and made somewhere in Quebec I believe, out of Canadian materials. My memory is that the price either on the dock at Quebec City or in France-I am not sure which-was approximately $2,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

speechtext:
That goes to show that a very good frame' house could be built for that money. My memory is that the walls of the house were papered in Canada, but perhaps the papering would need some touching up after the house was erected in France. That struck me as a mighty fine program, whoever in Canada promoted it. Perhaps the department did; at least they must have been told about it. I wondered then, and I have wondered since, why we could not have prefabricated houses in Canada. Most of the basements could have been made out of cement blocks They are easily made. While cement is not just a glut on the market, perhaps it can be obtained today in sufficient quantities to meet the demand for cement blocks for basements of houses.
When the minister closes the debate I should like him to tell the house why we cannot have prefabricated houses here in large quantities as they have them in England and France. A few moments ago an hon. member to my left said that England built a large number of houses in a certain length of time. I have forgotten the time, but I have given the figure before myself. At the moment I have not the figure in my mind. I do not just remember the length of time it took them to build their program of 750,000 houses.

National Housing Act
Knowing as I do that all the material used in the English houses and the French houses must come from outside these countries, because they have not the raw product supply, I ask myself why we are and have been in the position as to housing that we are in, in Canada today. The situation is nothing short of appalling. The part of the city of Toronto that I represent is thickly congested. I am proud to live in that part of the city. It is one of the largest workingmen's areas in the city. Quite a number of them work in the plant that I worked in for many years. I know that many, many of these houses are congested, with a large number of people in each one of them, far beyond what they were built for. Houses that were built to accommodate a family of five have at least ten people crowded into them today. It therefore looks to me as if, in the future, hundreds of thousands of new houses will have to be built for the people now living under such congested conditions.
A short time ago an hon. member referred to Quarrels among families, between landlords and tenants and so on, because of the congestion. Is it any wonder? I have been in many houses. I am going home tonight. On Saturday I hope to pay visits to various parts of the riding I represent. I love going among the ordinary folks and seeing the conditions under which they live. I have seen conditions that I just cannot describe. From what I have seen I know that for a long time to come in Canada there will be a great demand for houses.
I hope that the minister who did such a good job in making munitions during the war, turning out guns and tanks, ammunition and ten thousand and one different things that entered into the prosecution of the war, can do a good job in this respect as well. We all know he did a good job during the war. I for one hope that he will take hold of this big problem, turn over a new leaf altogether and go to work, because this problem is too big to be solved by ordinary methods. I ask him to start in again as he did when he took over the job of building guns, tanks and other war weapons, and construct houses in Canada, not by the thousands but by the tens of thousands, because there must be a market for 150,000 or
200,000	houses in Canada. I believe the minister can do it, if he would only carry on in the same manner as he did during the war.
I do not believe in censuring the minister. He has had a big job to do, and he has done a big job. I am one of those who believe he can do a gigantic job of building houses. If they can build 750,000 houses in England in two or three years, why cannot we do the
same thing in Canada? We do not have to go out of Canada to get the material; it is all here. Lumber and cement are here in quantities sufficient to build houses, and that is the immediate job to be done. I for one am going to look to the minister to overcome the difficulty, to surmount the obstacles. The situation is bad.
I listened to the minister yesterday and when he finished I said to myself-and this is no reflection on him-there is not a thing in the program for the average man and woman whom' I represent. There may be something in it for those who can pay $80 a month rent. I do not know many of these in my riding. In my riding, generally from 350 to 500 people live in a block. They are not living there at $80 a month. The couple to whom I referred on a street in my riding could only pay $22 a month rent. Therefore, when the minister suggested yesterday that folks could pay $80 a month or that a house costing $6,800 would be let for $37.50 a month, he was not speaking of the people in my riding. I would not name the streets, but A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J, K, L, M, N streets in my area in Toronto have on the average 350 and more people living in one block. Of that number, five out of twenty-five could pay $37.50 a month; the others just cannot do so. It cannot be done today on the wages they are getting, because wages are not anything like what some folks think they are. Too many of them are out of work; too many of them are unwell; too many of them have been getting sick; too many of them have a thousand and one troubles, and they just cannot pay $37.50 a month.
What is the average man and woman going to do? He can pay rent for a house that could be built for $2,500. These lovely houses I saw on the docks in Quebec City being shipped to France, and the picture I saw the other day of houses being erected in England are the houses I have in mind. The pictures showed a dozen giant lorries going along some road in England, and each lorry carried a full prefabricated house. If they can do it over there we can surely do it here. We should do it in defence of the health of our people. The health of the people today is deteriorating. That is indicated by the poor man I spoke of a few minutes ago who died a couple of days ago. He was quite hale and hearty when I saw him two weeks ago, but not just in the best of health, because his spirit had broken down owing to the conditions under which he was living.
I am sure that the country will support the minister in some gigantic housing program if he will bring forward a bill to have houses
National Homing Act

built for not more than $2,500 to $3,000 apiece. It can be done, but the way we are doing it today it takes too 'long to erect the ordinary house. I visited two or three areas around Toronto in which quite a large number of houses are being erected. At the speed at which they are being erected, Your Honour, they cannot be built for less than $5,000 or $6,000. The average workingman cannot finance a house at that price. It cannot be done. I know too many of them,; I worked with too many of them, and therefore I say it cannot be done. I am satisfied that if the minister will take the bit in his teeth and bring in a program to build houses by the countless thousands on some new program such as he organized for the building of guns and tanks and so forth, houses can be built on a prefabricated basis for the ordinary workingman for not more than $3,000 apiece. The average workingman can finance that.
When the minister finished his remarks yesterday I said to myself, this bill does not give any hope to the renter. The renter cannot pay $80 a month, and the average workingman cannot pay $37.50 a month. It does not give any hope to the owner, because the average workingman cannot afford to buy a house at $6,800. He would lose his house. I remember very well that in my part of the city a multitude of people lost their homes during the depression, homes which did not cost over $2,500 to erect in that area.
I should like to see the minister revise the whole program and bring in something such as he did during the war. We did a gigantic job then and we have as big a job now, because this is worse than war to the average working man whose family are being scattered all over the city. We should begin a real program to provide homes for the people.
Something was said yesterday about guaranteeing two per cent on the investment in the building of houses. I do not know of anyone who would build houses on two per cent return. I own a number of houses myself and I know of the trials and tribulations I have with some of them. Indeed I would be glad to sell every one of them now if I could and get rid of the worry. I cannot dream of anyone undertaking to build a house with two per cent on the investment, certainly not a house costing $6,800. It cannot be done.
The last few days, I received two or three letters from people who use a good deal of gyproc, and they told me that the regulations of last November-I suppose they referred to what was done by the Minister of Finance- had seriously interfered with their importations of this material. It is most unfortunate that we have to import gyproc, because it can

be made in huge quantities in Canada. Every province in Canada can make gyproc, and it is important in the construction of prefabricated houses, so that if we do go into the business of building houses on a large scale there should be some provision for keeping up a supply of gyproc.
I know the minister can do this. During the war he did a spiendid job, as I have said. He did a good job in producing guns. I see my hon. friend the member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross) looking at me. In his own city there was a gigantic plant built, the Westing-house establishment, I believe. I went to see it myself. I should like to have the minister tell us, when he speaks in reply, why he cannot do the same job today in the production of houses in a large way.
If it is authority the minister wants, I for one would vote him that authority so that our people can have a chance to live. I would not undertake to describe their living conditions today. The people I come in contact with, the people I am talking about now, are not the rich class of people represented by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) or the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross). The people in those districts have fine homes. The men and women I am thinking about are the multitudes living in Davenport riding, in West Toronto, Trinity and Spadina. There they are in countless thousands packed in close together, many wanting homes. The conditions under which too many have to live are such as no human being ought to be asked to put up with.
I am not going to say much more. As I said at the beginning, I was one of those who felt, when the minister was appointed, knowing his capacity and his experience as a builder, that he would do a big job. Something has prevented him. What it is I do not know and I should like him to tell us. I believe he can do the job. I will not censure him in any way, because there is some reason why he has not done it, but the program now before us will not go very far in solving the housing problem.
The rent rate is too high. The cost of building is too high. We have to get down to a program such as they have in France and England. The minister nodded his head a few moments ago when I referred to houses that I had seen on the dock at Quebec City. Those were smart houses. I went through one and was well pleased. They were well built, well put together. It is a credit to France, and I am sure the French people are taking advantage of it.
The program announced by the minister yesterday will not be satisfactory. I appeal

Speaker's. Ruling
to him to do whatever has to be done to promote a genuine housing program. I believe he is capable of doing a job of the proportions of the job he did during the war. At that time he produced all that was necessary for the men to fight, which resulted in winning the war. Let us win the peace by providing homes at a reasonable rent and homes at low cost to the average working man, not men who can pay $6,800, which is beyond the vast majority of the people I represent, but men who want houses costing $3,000 and no more. I am one who believes the minister can do the job.

Mr. Speaker, I do not often take part in a debate on housing, but coming from a city where there has been a housing crisis for years I feel that I must speak in this debate.
In so far as this resolution is an outline of the government's housing policy for 1948, I want to tell the minister that it does not come anywhere near meeting the housing needs of this country. Moreover, in my opinion this outline of policy will come as a shocking disappointment to those people who have clung to the hope that the federal government would assume its responsibility in the matter of housing. Instead of this being an indication that the government is going to assume its responsibilities in that regard, it is the final act of abdication of government responsibility for housing. It is done on the assumption that by various guarantees home building can be made attractive to what I think the minister

National Housing Act
called yesterday professional landlords and investors. If the minister expects private enterprise to provide homes for the people of Canada, he is leaning on a broken reed.
The housing situation in Canada today is not something that developed either during or since the war. There was a housing shortage in Canada before the war began. What has happened since is that the housing shortage has become worse, and it still is becoming worse every day. Private enterprise cannot today and will not today provide homes for the people who need them most. If there is anything clear in the housing picture, that is it.
Let me draw the minister's attention to a few facts. In 1943 a committee, known as the Curtis advisory committee on reconstruction, was appointed to look into the housing situation. That committee reported on March 24, 1944. After outlining the housing situation in Canada, it made certain recommendations. For instance, at page 12 of the report it recommended the building of 606,000 urban units and
125.000	rural units in the first ten years following the war. That is, it proposed that, in order to meet the national requirements in housing, 731,000 units would be required in the first ten years following the war. In addition to that, I believe the report said that some 60,000 units would be necessary every year to meet the accumulating housing needs.
Then at page 13 the committee pointed out that there were many houses requiring substantial improvements and repairs. Of these there were 355,000 in the urban centres and
188.000	in rural areas, or a total of 543,000
homes in need of substantial improvements or repairs. That was the situation as it was found in 1943 and reported upon in 1944, at a time when the war had been in progress for about four years.	[DOT]
The minister said yesterday that in 1947 there were 77,000 units completed. I imagine that also some improvements have been made and some repairing has been done. In another -portion of his speech the minister said that building was catching up with housing needs. He did not say, however, how many houses had been demolished in the last year. Going around Vancouver and Ottawa, I can see that great numbers have been torn down because of their becoming obsolete or being unfit for human habitation.
At page 14 the Curtis report says that tenants in the lowest income group, which constitutes one-third of the population, should not pay more than $12 a month. I realize that since 1944 there has been some increase in wages and in the cost of living, so that if we increase that figure by, say 50 per cent, we 5849-233i
would have today a rent of $18 a month. Where in this measure is provision made for that third of the population who cannot pay more than $18 a month in rentals? What authority is providing homes for that part of the population?
Let me point out that that is the segment of the population which needs to be provided for. Once we get above that, we get closer to the people who are able to provide housing accommodation for themselves.
Perhaps you would call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
