Mr. Mac.INNIS: Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was pointing out that what is needed at the present time in the way of a housing policy is a low-rental housing program and that such a program demands federal subsidies of one kind or another. But there is very little in the statement made by the minister yesterday to indicate that there is any intention on the part of the government to go ahead with a low-rental housing program. Unless we do that, we shall never have a housing program in Canada that will meet the needs of the people. That was the finding of the Curtis committee, and I should like to read three or four paragraphs from its report. At page 18 of the report the Curtis committee says:
Low-Rental Housing
A complete revision of part II of the National Housing Act should be undertaken with a view to the inauguration of a comprehensive low-rental housing program.
Again:
Local housing authorities should be established as the agencies for the operation of low-rental housing projects in the areas concerned.
Again:
Loans for capital costs for low-rental undertakings should be provided directly by the dominion government, at the lowest possible interest rates, desirably the current rate for long-term government bonds plus a small charge for administration.
Again at page 19:
The subsidies required for the purpose of permitting rentals to be set lower than the economic or commercial level should be provided by the dominion government in the form of annual grants. These would be made to local housing authorities for projects defined by reference to the income limits of the tenants and the construction costs of the projects.
The Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities in their last report make somewhat the same proposals, and the minister yesterday, at page 3642 of Hansard, had this to say in regard to those proposals:
The Canadian federation of mayors has already sent us a brief concerning low-rental housing. Their proposals have merit but are not acceptable in their present form chiefly because they contemplate full financing by the dominion government both in respect to capital costs and operating deficits.
In his statement yesterday, the minister said that an assisted national housing program should be in concert with the three levels of government. With that I absolutely agree because administration and other factors make

such co-operation desirable. But under their present system of raising money the municipalities cannot provide funds for that kind of social work; I insist that housing is not only an economic question but a social one as well. If the funds are not provided, the people as a whole, who ultimately pay for everything, will have to pay for the lack of proper housing in other ways. I quote further from page 193 of the Curtis report:
One of the blind spots in thinking of housing policy is the belief that low rents mean rents of the order of $20-25 or even more, when considerably lower figures are necessary, for unskilled and low-wage workers, workers whose employment is irregular, or families with more than the average number of children. Until this perspective is righted, progress in catering for the needs of this section of the population, some of which is rural as well as urban, can hardly be expected.
What the Curtis report said in that regard is just as true today, if not more so, as it was when the report was made in 1944. It would be expected that the government, having set up this committee, which made a comprehensive report, would pay some attention to it and that the National Housing Act would, over the years, be amended accordingly; but so far as any amendments have been made since to the National Housing Act, they have been in a direction away from, rather than toward, the recommendations of the Curtis report.
In 1946 or 1947, I am not sure which, the minister made a statement in the house in regard to Housing Enterprises Limited, a group of insurance companies made proposals for building houses that could be rented for from S32.50 to $35 a month. On May 29, 1947, at page 3596 of Hansard the minister said this:
It (Housing Enterprises) was formed to build low-cost housing. The government has never been happy about that phase of the project. Even in its early stages it seemed doubtful whether it was building a class of * housing that this government should endorse as being in the low-rental area.
That is, at the beginning when the units were to be let for $32.50 to $35 a month.
However, the insurance companies had for years been bringing pressure on the government to end government construction. It was claimed that this was a field which should be left to private enterprise. The government has always countered with the answer: if that is your field, why not take some direct part in it? Housing Enterprises was started as a private venture with the support of the federal government and by invitation of the federal government. The results have been becoming less and less satisfactory. When the decision was made by the insurance companies-not by the government- that activity in this field should be ended, the government had no objection.

National Housing Act
The insurance companies, which have been providing some of the money for this sort of building, had been urging the government to get out of the housing business and let them do the job, and when the government let them do it, and gave them a loan of some $45,000,000 to boot, in a very short time they threw up their hands.
Speaking in the house on May 14, 1947, at page 3070 of Hansard the minister said:
Last fall Housing Enterprises accumulated land for their 1947 program. The unsatisfactory nature of many of their 1946 cost-plus contracts made it prudent for Housing Enterprises to require that their 1947 program be carried out on the basis of firm bids. A firm bid has been received for some 400 units in Hamilton at a price which would result in rentals of $55, $65 and $75 for three-, four- and five-roomed units respectively. Housing Enterprises feel that the purpose for which they entered the field is not being fulfilled, and that rentals which result from such high cost are far in excess of those which the scheme envisaged. Unless it is possible for Housing Enterprises to secure considerably lower prices on other projects, they do not intend to proceed with their 1947 program.
With that experience of private enterprise in home building, we find the minister saying yesterday that it was the intention of the government to get out of the home construction business as quickly as possible and to encourage private enterprise to take over. He said, as reported on page 3641 of yesterday's Hansard:
The dominion government is in the direct rental housing field because neither private enterprise nor other levels of government is providing greatly needed rental housing accommodation. I look forward to the day when the dominion may withdraw from the field of direct house building. Therefore we are anxious to do everything we can to encourage more private house building. The proposal before the house is designed to make rental housing more attractive to professional landlords and investors.
With the experience that my right lion, friend has had with private enterprise since 1945 in the building of houses and the results that have been achieved, and particularly with the results that have been achieved so far as low-rental housing is concerned, does he now expect that private enterprise can provide homes for the people in this country who need low-rental housing?

speechtext:
The housing situation throughout the whole of Canada is most deplorable. I hold in my hand a report made by a committee on housing in Vancouver under date of January, 1948, and I wish to quote a short paragraph from it, namely, the statement of the social service administrator for the city of Vancouver. He said, in regard to housing:
' The situation has greatly deteriorated during the past year (that is 1947). Low-rental housing is not available and social allowances and pensions are so far below the level of economic rentals that it is useless to hope that private landlords will rent quarters at the rates our clients are able to pay. In. one instance a woman with two children, whose normal social allowance is $50 monthly, was persuaded to move from a shack which resembled a discarded packing case, and the only accommodation she could find was two rooms at a rental of $35 a month. To the normal shelter rate of $13 the department added $22. monthly. This ease and many others like it indicate the need for subsidized housing units where adequate accommodation could be provided at lower costs than is now paid for the maintenance of slums.
I would urge not only the minister and the government but this house to see to it that provision is made to house the people of this country properly. If such provisions are not made we shall pay for the lack of them in other ways that will be much more expensive in the long run than if we provided decent homes.
National Housing Act

The minister mentioned yesterday that we were catching up somewhat on the housing program. I quote again from this report:
Taking the city of Vancouver alone, the population increased last year (summer 1946 to summer 1947), by 14,800 persons, requiring, on the basis of 3-2 persons per family, some 4,600 additional housing units. New dwellings completed during the year ended December, 1947, totalled 2,669, showing a deficit of nearly 2,000 units. This figure takes no account of deterioration or demolition of existing dwellings. It is evident therefore that the enormous backlog of building, estimated at over 20,000 houses for the city alone in 1945, is not merely" not being reduced, but is steadily increasing.
In the face of conditions of that kind, what effect will this program have? What effect will the government's policy have?

I cannot explain that, except I suppose the fear of the authorities of Vancouver to incur expenses which, in a few years, might become a financial burden. I quite appreciate the efforts the minister has made during the past few years to get the city of Vancouver to take even a small part of the responsibility" for housing, and I have criticized the city for not doing its share. I mentioned a moment ago that I did agree with the minister that a proper national housing scheme must be, because of conditions in Canada, on the three government levels.
The minister referred to the recommendations of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities. I have their program before me and I should like to quote three short paragraphs from the report:
The inescapable fact about low-rent housing is that, no matter what economies may be effected or how low-cost the project may be, there will be some families who are unable to afford the economic rent which such accommodation requires in order to support its capital costs and carrying charges.
And the next paragraph:
An annual rental subsidy (of one form or another) has come to be almost universally" recognized as the best and most practicable technique for overcoming the problem. It is the basic principle now incorporated in the low-rent housing legislation of the United Kingdom, the United States. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Sweden.
"A rental subsidy has the merit of being flexible and subject to variation if circumstances or experience demand. It is straightforward in effect, and understandable as a rent-reduction fund applied to a clear-cut social welfare purpose."

That is the statement of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities:
The last paragraph is from the Curtis report and is included in the recommendations of the Canadian federation of may'ors and municipalities.
I ask the house to look at this matter, not only as a housing problem but also as a social problem, and in that connection I wish to quote one further statement, this time from the report of the community chest and council of greater Vancouver for May, 1947. With reference to housing, there is the following statement:
Inadequate housing leads to breakdown in physical and mental health, strained family *relationships, behaviour difficulties, both of a minor and serious nature, and juvenile delinquency. When placement of children has to be made away from parents there is a loosening of family ties and damage to the normal development of the child's personality. This is particularly .true of the pre-school child ... In cases where the parents have had the problems of inadequate housing, high rent and low income, their sense of responsibility must be strong to overcome their problems and reunite the family. It appears obvious that provision of adequate housing is a cheaper measure than having to maintain citizens in hospitals, jails, detention homes, foster homes and mental hospitals. We all know that the cost in money of such curative and palliative measures is great. The cost in human values and human happiness is much greater and cannot be measured in terms of dollars and cents.
In conclusion I wish to say that I endorse everything that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) said this afternoon about the minister's abilities in handling measures of the kind we are now discussing. I would say to the minister and to the house that, in view of the desperate need of the people of Canada for housing, in view of the evidence already" available that private enterprise cannot and will not provide homes for the great bulk of the Canadian population who need it most, the resolution now before us is not worthy of the minister who introduced it. It is not the way' in which he set out to provide the sinews of war for many of those who now find themselves without homes. It should, in my opinion, be withdrawn and a more adequate program introduced.

Mr. Speaker, Samuel Johnson yvrote that praise, like gold and diamonds, owes its value only to its scarcity. As I have but little praise to offer this evening, I shall keep that precept in mind. Nor have I any inconsiderate or bitter reproaches to direct to anyone. I rise only to

National Housing Act
complete certain statistics, to correct one or two points in the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Hamel). I recall the Cartier election, when the labour progressive party candidate was opposing two other candidates.
I took part in this fight which took place, I believe, in 1943. In the matter of demobilization, referred to by the hon. member, I must say that it ended in fact on September 1, 1947, because of the fact that the non-permanent service was then in effect.
I shall not indulge in particularly bitter reproach, Mr. Speaker. However, in seeking to excuse the provincial or municipal governments which prefer not to handle the housing problem, the hon. member said that the federal government had made a mess of the situation and that it is rather difficult now for these other governments to solve this problem, or to have their autonomy respected.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that autonomy can apply both ways. I know that during the war the dominion government took a special and direct interest in the building of houses. Since the war is over, normally the provincial and municipal governments should immediately have claimed their autonomy and should have set to work. However, the dominion agreed to build houses, not to favour any province in particular, but the country as a whole. If my memory serves me right, the hon. member quoted statistics to show that building had decreased. In my opinion, if building appears to have slowed down, it is because the figures he quoted included not only dwellings, but various war plants erected during the last war, a fact that the hon. member forgot to mention. That is why his statistics are not entirely fair to those who build houses. I have here a table showing the number of houses built during the war compared to the total number built during the period from 1945 to 1947. In 1941, during the war, 48,000 houses were built while 40,000 were completed in 1942,
36,000	in 1943 and 39,000 in 1944 which comes to 163,000 dwellings for the war years, .this figure not including war plants. On the other hand, here are approximate though fairly accurate figures on Canada's post-war housing achievement: 48.000 dwellings were built in 1945, 67,000 in 1946, and, according to the latest statistics, 78,000 in 1947, so that almost 190.000 houses were completed in this period. From 1941 to 1947, the Wartime Housing Limited, a crown corporation, put up 31,192 houses. You will grant, Mr. Speaker,
that if failure there is, it is a failure from which those concerned have obtained a rather nice cut. However, and this happens very often, there are some who pocket no more than 10 per cent to 15 per cent. I realize that it is quite a problem but one must keep in mind various factors such as time, place and even climate. I heard the hon. member compare our housing program with home-building in England. When my hon. friend reaches LaTuque at 2 o'clock in the morning at forty below zero weather to tour the northern part of his constituency, I am sure that he would not want to leave a coach that had been built for the English climate, nor would he like to put up at a hotel.
So I say that the construction of Canadian houses cannot be compared to that of English houses. The construction of Canadian houses requires more care; walls and foundations have to be much thicker and more damp-proof. That type of construction therefore calls for a lot more building materials, and greater care on the part of the builders. Besides, it must not be assumed that a country with a budget like ours and a population like ours can build as many houses as a country with a budget much higher than ours and where the housebuilders show only half the care of our own builders. Comparisons are odious. My hon. friend will remember that saying which he often heard while he attended the seminary. The hon. member has perhaps been in Europe. Houses over there are quite unlike ours. In Italy houses seem to be built to stand anything. When the weather is damp, they do not feel it over there as we do in our Canadian houses. One advantage is that they do not need a heating system. Sometimes they have a fire-place, but that is all. But they do not build with the same care as we do here. So there is no comparison.
We must not forget either that during the war, and especially towards the end, from 1944 to 1947, numerous strikes broke out in this country. My hon. friend knows that. These strikes paralysed production, especially that of building materials, including steel. What with strikes on the one hand, and a rush of builders on the other, the building industry was bound to feel the effects of this shortage. No country could expect to solve this difficulty faster than we have. My hon.
National Housing Act

friend who is well-read, is undoubtedly aware that there is not another country in Europe or indeed in the wrorld, whose post-war reconstruction has progressed further than Belgium's. In order to arrive at the point where it finds itself now, Belgium was obliged to impose almost irritating restrictions on its people. Belgium has always wished to restore itself-too often had it acted as a shock absorber between two hostile nations-and has imposed sacrifices on itself to achieve that end. There was much criticism of course, but Belgium did, in fact, set the world an example which Canada has never ceased following to a certain extent. I can understand the hon. member claiming that the shortage of building materials was due to an excess of exports. I cannot blame him when he mentions England. I myself have often spoken of England and I have frequently stated that she was costing us a lot of money. On the other hand, he knows that I have changed my position regarding the two billion dollar loan. I looked upon the spreading of the communist tentacles over Europe as very disquieting. I could not let another country fall, another country which could prevent the spread of communism. Like a man who fears danger,

ucts, but I do not wish to detain the house longer than is necessary. The hon. members do me the honour of listening quite attentively to what I have to say, for which I thank them.
I now wish to criticize all those who build houses nowadays, the government and Wartime Housing Limited among others. The situation in Quebec is somewhat peculiar. It is, in fact, intolerable, since the houses that are being built there are too small. Whether we like it or not, the population of Quebec is certainly going to continue increasing. Our good Canadians of French descent, as well as those of Irish and Scottish stock, will continue to people the province of Quebec because they believe in it. I must say that the present government in Quebec may lose power at any time, but let it be. I contend that the houses built are not big enough. One way of preventing the spread of communism and satisfying the people is to give them good dwellings. We must be able to house the father, the mother and their ten or fifteen children, without compelling them to sleep two or three per bed. as I have often seen when I gave them medical assistance. It is imperative that we build bigger houses. Again I say-and I speak particularly to the youngest among us-that we have no intention of reducing the number of children in our families, because we have faith in this good old Canadian soil and wish to preserve the tradition of the province of Quebec, which has always overcome the difficulties it has found in its path.
