speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when Bill No. 176, to amend the National Housing Act, was before parliament a year ago, I stated on the 29th of May:
Indeed if it were not for the outstanding contribution the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply made during the war I would be pressing for his resignation on account of the housing conditions in Canada.
Nearly a year has passed since then, and relatively the housing situation is much worse today than it was a year ago. I do not think I have ever heard the minister make as weak an address to parliament as the one he made yesterday in streaking to this resolution. I have before me several reports published by the authority of the minister who is sponsoring this resolution. One is the story of Polymer ; another is the T.C.A. annual report; another the Canadian Mutual Aid report; and the annual report to the Minister of Reconstruction. of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
The minister risked his reputation and $50,000,000 of the taxpayers' money when he sanctioned the construction of the Polymer corporation. I was among the members of parliament privileged during the war to visit this project. Previously I have paid tribute to the minister for his courage and ingenuity in being responsible for the construction of what I understand is one of the most efficient synthetic rubber plants in the whole world. It is hard to exaggerate the part played by this industry in achieving the allied victory.
The annual report of the T.C.A. contains some interesting pictures. There is a picture of one of the North Stars bought by the minister for $600,000. There is a picture of the minister and the previous president of T.C.A. and party,
5849-234J
National Housing Act

after completing a record non-stop flight from Vancouver to Montreal in the space of six hours and fifty-two minutes.
The Canadian Mutual Aid board, of which the minister was chairman, tells something in its report of Canada's contribution to the allied victory by the distribution of mutual aid during the war. I find that contributions were made to Australia, totalling $91,000 000; the British West Indies, $5,000,000; China, $39,000,000; France, $25,000,000; India, $18,000,000; New Zealand, $15,000,000; U.S.S.R., $167,000,000; the United Kingdom, $2,112,000,000, and other contributions to UNRRA and others, making a total of $2,482,000,000.
When you compare those contributions made by the department under the supervision of the minister with the contributions made in the field of housing I am sure that the minister is not proud of this department which comes under his supervision.
I find that there are no pictures in the annual report of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The minister is not proud of the slum-like houses built during the war by Wartime Housing. I criticized the construction of those houses at the time, pointing out that, since this was the first major entry of the dominion government into the field of housing, it seemed a pity that potential slums should be built by the federal authority. The minister promised that these houses would be torn down within two or five years' time at the most after the ending of hostilities, but I contended what has proved to be a fact, that they would never be torn down so long as less desirable houses were being occupied in the various centres. Unfortunately, in every centre where wartime houses were built there will be for a very long time many less desirable houses occupied. So I repeat that wartime houses are potential slum dwellings.
The report has an interesting section dealing with the construction of rural housing. It mentions that section 14 of the National Housing Act, providing for loans to assist in the construction of rural housing, *was proclaimed by order in council on June 24, 1947. I might mention that the act was passed in 1944, so that it took four long years to get the government to pass an order in council finally to make this section of the act effective. Later on they were running out of material and you have a repetition of very much the same material. A couple of pages later, on page 9,

they go into quite a long discussion pointing out that, because of the Saskatchewan farm security act and its application to National Housing Act farm loans, no such farm loans will be made in Saskatchewan. It goes on;
Until satisfactory arrangements can be concluded with each of the governments of the prairie provinces to permit the use of a flexible payment plan for repayment of loans by farmers operating farms primarily grain-growing in character, the corporation is not willing to approve applications from this type of farm.
No loans in Saskatchewan, no loans in the prairie provinces. Nearly a whole page in the annual report tells of what the government is doing in the field of rural housing, and then at the last, at the bottom of page 9 I find this:
No applications for farm loans were received in 1947.
And so, after years and years, not a single five-cent piece is being made available by the federal government with a view to dealing with the urgent rural housing problems that I shall mention before I am through.
The speech delivered by the minister yesterday should be studied very carefully by everyone who looks for a solution of this problem of housing. At page 3639 of Hansard he points out;
I rvould point out, however, that the greatest demand and need is for rental housing. Many people buying houses are only doing so because they cannot secure rented accommodation.
That has been perfectly obvious for a long time. The housing situation is so acute that people have been obliged to pay two prices for houses to get some place to live. It is unfortunate that the young men who went from Canada and risked their lives during the war years and fought to save their homes should find, when they come back, that the government, which made such fine promises, has made no adequate provision to find them homes, and so they have had to go into debt, sell their chattels, mortgage their future and pay two prices for houses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: And they will never be able to pay for them.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Davenport points out, it will be physically impossible for many of these veterans to pay for them. I am told that there is quite a racket in Canada by organizations which are dealing in second mortgages. The demand for housing has been so great that in order to get a roof over their heads people will pay any price. They are able to get first mortgages at fairly low rates, but they must pay high rates to get second mortgages.

National Housing Act
36S3
On page 3640 of Hansard an interesting paragraph appears. The minister said:
In 1947 it became evident that Housing Enterprises could not produce housing at satisfactory cost levels. Housing Enterprises decided to abandon new projects in 1947 and limit their activities to the completion of the 3,313 units under construction.
I might suggest in passing, Mr. Speaker, that the minister should try to get Mr. Mansur, president of Central Mortgage and Housing, to use more original language in his annual reports rather than copy the words of the minister word for word. I am not going to take time to compare the paragraphs, but I think Mr. Mansur uses words almost identical with those of the minister. Let me remind the house that on July 22, 1946, the minister told the house of the wonderful plans that had been made to have rental housing built. He said as reported at page 3686 of Hansard:
hjext I would like to deal with the activities of Housing Enterprises of Canada, Limited. Hon. members will remember that at the last session of the house amendments were made to sections 9 and 11 of the National Housing Act whereby an institutional holding company could proceed with rental housing. Shortly after these amendments were passed, all life insurance companies operating in Canada joined together and formed a mutual institutional holding company in the name of Housing Enterprises of Canada, Limited. Housing Enterprises contemplated a two-year program of about 10,*900 units and planned to distribute the much-needed rental housing throughout the iirban communities from coast to coast. The financial arrangement is that loans are made to Housing Enterprises under section 9, as I have previously described, and the 10 per cent equity of Housing Enterprises comes under the provision of section 11 of this act.
On the next page the minister said:
I would like to express my appreciation, as well as that of the government, for the cooperation ^ of the life insurance companies in entering into the rental housing field at this time when conditions are so difficult.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) referred to the minister's reference to Housing Enterprises a year ago when it was fairly obvious that the set-up was on the way out. The minister said yesterday:
In August, 1947, the life insurance companies which owned Housing Enterprises, approached us to request that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation take over their operations. In light of all circumstances the government accepted this proposal. The corporation has taken over Housing Enterprises Limited and has completed and rented the 3,313 units in the thirty-two projects.
Two years ago the minister promised that the solution for rental housing had been proposed by the insurance companies who were so anxious to get into this field. Two years later Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation come to the government and asked the government to bail them out and take over the uncompleted projects. The hon. member for Vancouver East also referred to another part of the minister's speech which appears on page 3641 of Hansard.
The dominion government is in the direct rental housing field because neither private enterprise nor other levels of government is providing greatly needed rental housing accommodation.
Some of the United States magazines, Mr. Speaker, offer handsome prizes every month for the funniest articles that appear in print each month. I plan to send the paragraph which I have just read, and I offer to share proceeds with the minister if it is selected. The dominion government is now in this housing field, because no other government would do anything about it and private enterprise would not do anything about it, and the minister now looks forward to the day when the dominion can withdraw from the field. He is going to withdraw by guaranteeing that people who lend money will have their loans guaranteed for a long period, and I submit that that is a most amazing statement for any cabinet minister to make.
I argued all through the years that there was no reason why a government which could spend $50,000,000 on the Polymer Corporation or on organizing the transcontinental and the trans-Atlantic air service could not take the responsibility of going into slum clearing and low-rental housing projects. The amount of money that was spent by Canada on our mutual aid program, nearly $2,500,000,000, as compared with the amount of money we have lost on housing, is of interest. In the annual report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, we find that at the end of the year the net. losses paid out under the housing act amounted to $2,147. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that with Canada's housing situation as critical as it is, the government cannot be very proud of having lost less than $3,000 in trying to provide adequate housing for the people of the dominion.
I have spoken on this question of housing frequently in parliament, but I cannot claim to be an authority on the subject. Tonight I should like to call to witness important organizations in Canada and in the United States-I will not get across to Europe-to support the point of view that we have made from time
National Housing Act

to time that housing is Canada's No. 1 problem. The citizens of this country must be divided roughly into three groups: first, the group of people who can provide housing for themselves without any assistance at all; second, the group that will provide adequate housing if loans can be made available at reasonable rates of interest, such as has been done through the National Housing Act, and the third and largest group of all, as large as the other two groups put together, the people whose incomes, unfortunately, have been fixed at such low levels that it is phj'sically impossible for them to pay an economic rent for decent housing.
I should like to start with Halifax, Nova Scotia. Halifax had its citizens' local committee which presented its report some time ago, and this is the significant paragraph:
It is not a question whether we shall pay or shall not pay, it is a question of whether we shall pay blindly or intelligently, whether we 71av for better housing or for the damage done by that which is worse. Housing of the poor we are going to provide, let us make no mistake about that. It is only a question whether we shall house them in hospitals, mental institutions. reformatories and jails; or whether we shall house them in cleanly, light and sanitary surroundings where both body and soul will have a chance. Which shall it be?
The housing position in Vancouver has been carefully studied by a representative group of citizens in that city. I am not selecting these cities because they have unusual conditions. Every city in Canada has its blighted and slum areas. Some cities have been more courageous in examining the situation and placing the facts out in broad daylight, and some people in these cities have been agitating with a view to getting something done. The Vancouver group have prepared an interesting report, and the section on the cost of slums is significant. It reads as follows:
Health. While it is rarely possible to isolate completely the damage to health caused by housing from that which is attributable to other social evils connected wdth poverty, such as malnutrition. the sum total of statistical and medical evidence which has been accumulated in Tecent years is so overwhelming that the cardinal importance of bad housing as a source of ill health is now generally recognized.
It mentions that a great many people, because of the housing situation, have been forced to supplement their housing allowances by cutting down on food consumption, and goes on to say:
The vicious circle thus created can only be broken by a determined effort on the part of the community as a whole to raise the conditions of those who have fallen below a minimum standard of healthful living.

This report refers to the city of Cleveland where 12] per cent of the deaths from tuberculosis occurred in the slum area containing only 2-4 per cent of the population. In one of the poorer areas of Vancouver the death-rate from tuberculosis was 102 per 100,000 as compared with 35 in the remaining part of the city. That, I submit, is a matter of concern not only to the people in Vancouver but to Canadians in all parts of the country. Three times as many died from tuberculosis in the blighted areas of Vancouver as died in the rest of the city. In the Chinese section 285 died, twice as many as in the slum area. Infant mortality was 73 per 1,000 as compared with 30 in the rest of the city. This report deals with the death rate in Liverpool and in other British cities and throughout the world, and the evidence is that wherever you have slum areas you have an added cost in fire prevention, you have sickness and juvenile delinquency, all of which costs have to be borne by the rest of the people.
I urge that the minister instruct his officers to give careful consideration to this report on housing in Vancouver. For a number of years the chief inspector of the division of sanitation and housing of the city of Winnipeg has made interesting reports. Mr. Officer, when he was in charge of this division, made this statement in his report in 1942:
It is surely not too much to say that when our men on active service return to civil life they have a right to expect that decent living quarters for their future family life is available, or at least in process of construction.
Now, after many of the men are home, the situation is worse than ever. I have the last two reports here, and the report for 1947
states:
We say that the housing situation is somewhat worse than it was a year ago . . . With all the clamour and publicity that has attended this amount of construction, it still leaves untouched the basic need of decent housing accommodation for thousands of our citizens . . . It is impossible for the majority of comfortably established individuals to sympathize adequately with the appalling housing conditions of today, under which a considerable section of the population lives. Were it otherwise, the general complacency of the public would vanish in a manner bodeful of much, to the comfortably encysted traditionalists in public and private life.
I suggest that members of parliament and members of the cabinet should try for a year coming into Ottawa, limiting themselves to the average income of the average citizen of Canada. Let them try to find living accommodations, spending one-fifth of the average Canadian income for the housing. Let them

National Housing Act
try coming here, if they have children, to find living quarters where children are permitted.
I submit that if the minister of reeonstruc-' tion and the members of the cabinet were in closer contact with people who have been house hunting in this and other cities of Canada we would be taking more vigorous action to solve the problem.
Let me now refer to Toronto for a moment. Sometimes that city is called Toronto the good. I should like to refer to the report of the lieutenant governor's committee on housing in Toronto in 1934. The then lieutenant-governor of Ontario, who was one of our colleagues here for many years, the Hon. Doctor Bruce, was responsible for convening a representative committee, and in his remarks at a banquet he made this statement:
These areas of misery and degradation exert an unhappy environmental influence upon many of our citizens.
I was interested to know that the present hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell) was then president of the board of trade in Toronto and was one of the group of responsible citizens in Toronto who took an active part in preparing this report. A survey was made of some of the worst areas in the city, and it was found:
Of the 1,332 dwellings and 1,421 households covered by the survey,
Ninety-six per cent of the dwellings fell below minimum standard of amenities,
Seventy-five per cent of the dwellings fell below the minimum health standard, Forty-three per cent had no cellars. Twenty-eight per cent were in a bad state of repair and a further 53 per cent definitely in need of repairs,
Eight-two per cent had no method of central heating and depended on stoves,
Fifty-eight per cent were damp and 20 per cent of these dwellings were subject to flood. Nine per cent had no electricity,
Forty per cent had smells inside or out, Fifty-five per cent were verminous,
Fifty-nine per cent had no bath,
Twenty per cent had outside toilets and a further 19 per cent had unsatisfactory inside toilets.
And so on. That was in 1934 and these units which were examined in that year are still being occupied.
The board of trade recently entertained members of the House of Commons in Toronto, and I should like publicly to express my appreciation of their wonderful hospitality. They were to be commended for taking us on a comprehensive tour of the city, including not only Rosedale and the Forest Hill village but some of the slum areas. I wish to put in a word for my Toronto friends and to express the hope that the federal government will take
an interest in the slum-clearing program that Toronto has been discussing since 1934. It is not good enough to say that the government of Ontario and the city of Toronto have not made the necessary representations. The fact is that the government of Canada must take official responsibility for slum clearing and low-rental housing in Canada. It must take the initiative and Toronto the good would be an ideal place in which to start.
Time is moving on and I shall not be able to refer to some of the American cities which I should like to discuss-New York, Green Belt, New Haven, and some of the other cities there which I have visited. I visited those cities in order to see what they were doing in the matter of housing. The report from Los Angeles states:
The housing authority of the city of Los Angeles is a public body, corporate and political. It was created by the enactment of the California housing authorities law in 1938. It is not a department of the city government, but is a political subdivision of the state of California. It has direct lines to three governmental bodies, the city, the state, and the federal government. The housing authority was officially established in Los Angeles on June 2, 1938, by a resolution adopted by the mayor and the city council. The basic objectives of the housing authority are twofold:
First, to clear the sub-standard dwellings existing in the city of Los Angeles and second, to provide decent, safe and sanitary homes for the lowest income families living in sub-standard dwellings who are unable to afford decent accommodations at rents required by private enterprise.
In this report they satisfy the private builders, whom the minister is so anxious not to offend. They say:
The housing authority has established its maximum entrance rental in the public low-rent housing developments thirty-one per cent below the lowest rent at which private enterprise can profitably provide standard housing. By law it can only provide housing for those low income families living in sub-standard housing. For these two reasons competition with privately owned standard property is impossible.
I think it should be prefectly obvious that if Canada undertook a major low-rental subsidies housing program such as was proposed in the report of the advisory committee on reconstruction during the war, it would have a stabilizing effect on our whole economy. I might mention that back in 1934-35, when we had more than 1.000,000 unemployed, a group of businessmen took the trouble to come to Ottawa to appear before a parliamentary committee to outline plans they had to solve the unemployment problem by means of low-cost housing. They suggested that the government borrow money from the Bank of Canada and
National Housing Act

make it available for housing at 2 or 2i per cent, suggesting that the money that would be saved by undertaking a building program to produce 130,000 or 140,000 housing units in three years would take every able-bodied man's family off relief.
Before my time expires I would point out to the minister that there are a great many constructive proposals which have been made and which in my opinion should have been acted upon before now. I have here an article by Professor Arthur of the University of Toronto, who was a member of the committee responsible for drawing up this so-called Curtis report. In this article he says:
The desire for better housing, and better living standards generally is a post-war objective which is firmly rooted in the minds of people in all ranks of life. Construction work in the housing field can be of particular importance, both in providing employment opportunities for men demobilized from the armed forces, and for men released by war industries.
In his article he estimates the savings that would be effected if a large project could be undertaken rather than the building of individual houses. He suggests that if 100 dwellings were built, there would be a minimum saving of 10 per cent, a probable saving of 18 per cent and a maximum saving of 27 per cent; whereas if 1,000 dwelling units were built, there would be a minimum saving of 6 per cent, a probable saving of 20 per cent and a maximum saving of 35 per cent. But the government is not travelling in that direction. I received a letter from a builder in Edmonton who was complaining about the obsolete ideas that are still prevailing. He says:
The government is practically forcing old-fashioned methods on the building industry. If you choose to prefabricate parts of houses in a plant in order to achieve economies with machinery and production line techniques you are liable to federal sales tax of 8 per cent on some at least of the operations on the grounds that it is a manufacturing operation.
In this day and age I think it should be obvious that tremendous savings could be effected by building cupboards and a great many parts of houses inside in the wintertime, increasing the off-site work.
Professor Arthur has an interesting section on farm housing, in which he says:
We are inclined to assume too readily that the farmer and his family are happy with their outhouse, their oil lamps, lack of refrigeration and lack of bathing facilities, except where provided by a galvanized basin. Of the total farm dwellings in Canada (730,060), 677,100 or 92 - 7 per cent were without bathing facilities and 92 per cent lacked flush toilets.

That was when the last census was taken in 1941. The breakdown according to provinces is here. I will not take the time now to give it to the house. But'with over 90 per cent of the farm homes in this dominion without bathing facilities or flush toilets, one does not need to have much imagination to visualize what a tremendous stimulus would be given to the whole building trade if Canada would face up to solving its rural housing problem.
I have in my hand one of the reports from the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, entitled "Manpower and Material Requirements for a Housing Program in Canada." I should like to say to hon. members that this is an excellent study, showing what it would cost to undertake and complete 80,000 houses in Canada. The figures are as follows:
Materials	 $280,317,000
On-site labour	 200,227,000
Overhead and profits	 53,394,000
Total	 $533,938,000
That is for desirable standards. But if actual standards that we now use were employed, that amount could be written down to $440 million.
Then, over at page 66 of the book is given the amount of cement and the value in dollars that would be needed for this sort of project. I hope that businessmen across Canada will take a more active interest in trying to press the federal and provincial governments to enter this low-cost housing field in order to provide houses for people in the lower income brackets. The figures are as follows:
Cement, gravel and Sand	 $ 21,344,000
Brick, tile and stone	 13,920,000
Lumber and its products	 119,527,000
Lath, plaster and insulation materials	 31,693,000
Roofing materials	 8,109,000
Paint and glass	 8,978,000
Plumbing and heating equipment
[DOT]and fixtures	 52,050,000
Electrical equipment and fixtures 10,805,000 Other materials	 13,891,000
Total	 $280,317,000
The fact is that we have no shortage of any of these materials. For the minister to come to parliament and suggest that we are going to make it easier to get into the rental housing field, to provide rental housing that will be available at $75 and $80, is an insult to 75 per cent, yes, 85 per cent of the Canadian people. The only people who can take advantage of rentals of $75 and $80 a month are those who, somehow or another, would be able to find housing.

National Housing Act
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to urge that the minister withdraw his proposed legislation and bring in a bill outlining comprehensive planning of our resources and manpower, taking into account the needs for housing. When, during the war, a flying Catalina was required, the fact that it cost $250,000 did not cause the minister to hesitate. Why does he get up in parliament and say that $6,800 per unit is the maximum limit that Canada will go for housing? Who knows that $6,800 is the limit our resources will provide? We do not want housing again where it is possible to get men on relief to supplement their incomes by working for twenty cents an hour. We do not want painters to supplement their incomes while on relief by painting houses for a song. We want those who are engaged in the housing industry to be paid union wages so that they, too, can look forward, on their incomes, to having houses.
As the minister in charge of housing in New Zealand told us when he was here during the war, when he took over the responsibility for housing, his objective was to see that every family in New Zealand would have a house, that every family would have a garden, that every individual in New Zealand would have a room in the house that he could call his own. So I submit that the minister cannot wait until we have a depression and until prices go down before facing up to the job of providing houses. Without any further delay the minister should convene a conference of representatives of government on the dominion, provincial and municipal levels, to work out the techniques in connection with the administration and managing, with a view to getting a start in slum clearance, low-rental housing and farm housing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I rise at this time in the debate, Mr. Speaker, to offer a few observations. I hope to say something constructive to the minister in charge of housing. As has already been said this afternoon by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins), the type of house that was being built, the five-room or four-room house, is uneconomical and is one that would last a family for only a short time. By the very nature of things, young families ultimately require larger houses. I spoke some time ago on this question, and I suggested to the minister that if the government wanted to produce homes for people, perhaps the semi-detached brick house which could be erected quickly, easily and cheaply would be a far better home than the type of house that has been built.
If you happen to fly over the city of Toronto, you will find some small houses; they look like playhouses, built here and there. They look fine from the air, but I suggest to the minister that the reason for the shortage of houses in the city of Toronto today is the fact that this type of house has been built. I do not know why it has been built. I assume it is being built by private builders as well as by government agencies, but for some reason or another this type of house has become popular. I believe one of these houses is shown in the literature which is given out by the national housing administration. Everybody buys it simply because he cannot get anything else. If the type of house with six rooms could be built, I suggest that the extra room in this house would largely provide for the people who are now without homes in Toronto. I believe that the situation is probably somewhat better today than it was a year or two years ago, but there is still a great deal of distress in the city of Toronto because of the housing shortage. From my own experience, I know of a case where a man who is at the present time in a tubercular sanitarium, cannot come home because his wife and child are living in one room alone. They need a house badly; yet they can neither get into their own house nor rent another one at a reasonable figure.
In Toronto, according to statistics which I believe to be correct, the number of persons per unit of housing is no greater now than it was in 1940, and probably no greater than during the worst of the depression. In greater Toronto in 1939, with a population of 868,000, some 200,000 housing units were available. In 1947, with an increase of 14-5 per cent in population to 993,000, there were 232,000 housing units, so that really the number of persons per unit has not increased. It is the distribution that is bad.
In this house I have called upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), then Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, to put into effect the emergency legislation and compel people to share their a-ccommodation. I know it is not very nice for a person with a large house and a small family to have to share it, but if that legislation were put into operation I do not believe it would have to be used very much, because the situation would right itself by the very force of circumstances. Arrangements would be made by owners of large houses to bring people into their homes, which would mean that other accommodation would become available. A government that prevents a man from getting into his own home, which he has bought and paid for and badly needs* could just as easily use the emergency legisla-
National Housing Act

tion that is still in force to make available surplus accommodation in cities like Toronto.
I have said that the five-room house is not an economical design; indeed it is the most expensive. In the first place, a five-room house all on one floor is most uneconomical because it requires a large roof and large foundation, two expensive parts of a house. A six-room house requires no more public utilities. The same water main will do for six rooms as well as for four or five rooms. The same plumbing will do, and the same furnace, so that the actual cost of a six-room house as compared with a five-room house is not much greater, even if it were all on one floor. After all, to make a house four feet wider only means eight feet more of wall, and a very small amount of plastering, flooring and all the other things that go into a house. Every room has a door, and that door will do for a large room as well for a small one. So, from the point of view of economical building, the cost does not increase proportionately with the size of the house.
That is true of a one storey building. When you come to a two-storey home you have a smaller roof and a smaller foundation, and you have a house which can be subdivided more conveniently. In Toronto these five-room houses are all they can buy, unless they find an older house; and often when people buy one of these five-room houses they have to leave some of their relatives behind, because there is no place for them. As the hon. member for Parkdale pointed out this afternoon, a five-room house is meant for a family of only three, or at the most four; the couple themselves and a boy or a girl, or two boys or two girls. It is uneconomical in every respect; and even at that these houses cost so much that the poorer people of Toronto cannot afford to buy them.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: If I may interrupt, our experience has been quite the reverse. We did build six-room houses at one time. In the early days we gave preference to four-room and six-room houses, and the four-room houses were by far the most popular. In many places six-room houses were difficult to rent. The five-room house was a compromise, which seems to have the most popular appeal. That is the reality of the situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: My experience would be entirely different.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is theorizing, is he not?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No, I am not; I know what I am talking about. I know how the old six-room houses sold, and that people who bought them were able to obtain some

revenue by renting the upstairs. It is impossible to sublet part of a five-room house which is all on one floor. I should like to know where in Toronto six-room houses were built by Wartime Housing.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: They were not built in Toronto. Toronto has built fewer houses in proportion than any city in Canada. The reason is that there is practically no land in Toronto on which to build houses.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: If you speak of Toronto itself that may be true, but if you speak of greater'Toronto, while we have the lake on one side, there is unlimited land on the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Try to build houses there. Your experience may be better than mine.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I know something about building in Toronto. I know that in the township of York, close to the city, where they have water mains and sewers and all the utilities, and where land is available, they refused to allow the dominion to erect these houses because they would not conform to their fire by-laws. The dominion wanted to build frame houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Then your theory is that the dominion must meet the views of the municipality, rather than the municipality meeting the views of the dominion?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am trying to answer the minister's statement that six-room houses were not popular, and that there was no land available in Toronto. There is plenty of good land, but the dominion did not buy good land. Wherever there was a little valley between a couple of hills, that was the land the dominion bought. The people are out there in mud during the spring and fall, and it will never be a really good residential district. I can tell you where one of those places is. It is just north of Weston. The dominion bought the worst land they could find. They went miles from good transportation when there was plenty of land available close to the city of Toronto, with all the public utilities necessary to make livable homes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: If my hon. friend would make some of that land available to Wartime Housing we would like to put some houses on it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: If Wartime Housing will come to me in Toronto I can give them a great deal of help.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: But perhaps my hon. friend prefers just to talk about the matter.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I should know something about it. I have been in Toronto for forty-six

National Housing Act
years; I have practised law there. I have some idea not only of housing at the present time but of housing following the first great war, of housing following the boom which burst in 1913, and some idea of the housing situation in Toronto following the 1890 boom.
Mr. HOWE; I have built only forty thousand of them in the last five or six years.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
You mean acting on
behalf of the Dominion of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is what I complain about; in my opinion you have not made a good job of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I would like the benefit of your broad experience, just the same.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I am only interested in behalf of the people who want houses.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What would be my interest, do you think?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Perhaps we are both interested in the same thing and are going at it in different ways. I am making suggestions which I believe are absolutely correct. The minister thinks differently, but I am sure he is wrong, because I know people want homes. At times in Toronto today when they want to get into homes they have bought they will say to the tenant, "Keep four rooms and give me two." I will admit that these are mainly the older houses, which have at least six rooms. You will find very few five-room cottages in older Toronto. In my own riding of High Park I suppose there must be twenty thousand houses, but I do not believe there are five hundred one-storey five-room houses among them. The houses are principally of the semi-detached type, with good people living in them.
After all, as the last speaker said, it is the people in the very low income brackets who want these homes in the worst way, and how can they pay 86,500, 87,500 or 88,500 for a little box of a house which would not be big enough for a family of any size? They do not want hardwood floors; they do not want all these fine things. They want a home to go to live in. I can say to the minister, who built 40,000 houses since then, that after every other depression there were always houses built, not completely finished. People went out and built their own homes. Perhaps they did not always have foundations under them. I think they made a mistake in that respect, because it costs more to do that after the house is built thrn before.
However, they built their own homes of five or six rooms, and started with those homes. It was a place to live in.
Today those homes will sell for almost anything, to people who can buy them. They are places to live in-and today they want places to which they can go. Unfortunately, the government in this building crusade upon which it has entered has tried to build small finely finished houses. They have waited for months to get plumbing for those houses. A person can, on the outskirts of Toronto, be without plumbing for a short time, so long as he has a place to sleep. They want places to which they can go, so that they will have something over their heads.
For this reason I say the government has made a tremendous mistake in building that type of house. These are frame houses, by the way. Frame houses, as a rule, use lumber which should be used in other parts of the house. There has been a shortage of material, in spite of what anybody says. There is a shortage of material and there has been a tremendous increase in the price of building materials.
What has been the cause of this increase in prices? I can give the answer to that. A booklet has been sent out by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, dated January,
1948.	It goes on, with a great deal of pride, to tell what they have done for business people. It tells of the millions of dollars spent to build factories and other commercial places. They take it as a matter of pride that they have allowed 81,400,000,000 in depreciation to help in connection with the building of those factories and commercial houses.
The minister may say that is a good thing. It is; but not a good thing when you have competition with the building of private homes. The people have to have houses to live in; that is absolutely necessary. The building of factories, et cetera, should have been postponed until a later date, when the people had their homes provided for them. At that time the building of these factories could have been provided as, in fact, the minister indicated was the intention, so as to take up the slack at the time when there might be a recession. Unfortunately, however, he has gone ahead, and he has guessed wrongly. He thought the recession was coming sooner, and he allowed these factories to go ahead and to use up all the available materials for that type of building.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am the only one who guessed right. I am the only man in this house who predicted that there would not be a depression after the war. Every Tory stood
National Housing Act

up and talked about the depression which would follow the war. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do.
Mr. MeMASTER: I did not hear what the minister said, but I did understand him to say that he predicted a depression.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I say that I was the only man in the house who has not predicted a depression.
Mr. MeMASTER: If you have not, then you have taken the very best means to see that, when a depression does come, it will be a very bad one; because you have spent the money, in a time like this.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
You are predicting one now, are you? May I ask my hon. friend a question?
Mr. MeMASTER: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Does he say that when the war ended we should not have permitted any industrial construction at all in Canada, and that we should turn all hands to work at building houses? I would like him to answer that question yes or no. He is, in my opinion, making a very absurd speech.
Mr. MeMASTER: I cannot say yes or no, because there may have been some that were absolutely necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I see.
Mr. MeMASTER: But I venture to say there was very little of it that was absolutely necessary. I say that people who had gone on manufacturing in a plant for many years could have continued without difficulty for several years longer without a new building, and it would have affected nobody's health. In the meantime these homes could have been built for people to live in.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No trouble about employing the million of people then engaged in war work?
Mr. MeMASTER: I am talking about something I know a little about.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, I have been carrying the responsibility for employment in this country for several years. I don't know the first thing about it!
Mr. MeMASTER: The minister said there was something he did not know a thing about. Well, it is interesting to know that. I should like him to say now what it is, because I do not think I could sleep without knowing what it was that he did not know anything about.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I said that I had been carrying the responsibility for seven or eight years, 
and I did not know the first thing about it. My hon. friend can tell me all about it at this stage.
Mr. MeMASTER: Well-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
And he is glad to do it.
Mr. MeMASTER: The responsibility for carrying on during seven or eight years has not been the responsibility of building houses. After all, a man can have so much responsibility that he cannot look after everything. I got on my feet to offer some constructive criticism because-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
And in my opinion you are offering something very silly.
Mr. MeMASTER: -it is my duty as a member of parliament to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Very silly.
Mr. MeMASTER: With regard to the minister's program concerning housing, commercial building and other types of building, may I say I have seen a report made by the building commissioner for the city of Toronto in which he says that very few houses-only some few hundred-are being built in Toronto proper, as distinct from the suburbs. But up to May 1, or about May 1, 1947, $21,000,000 worth of permits had been taken out for commercial and other buildings, other than houses. With that competition between the building of factories and the building of houses, what is the inevitable result? Prices have gone up. Materials have been scarce. As a result, the houses which people are going to buy today are at prices which are simply ridiculous. They will lose those houses, as sure as your life. The government, after all, will take losses-and perhaps they can stand it. But the people will lose those houses, and all the money they have put into them.
I see them buying these new houses at around $8,500-five-roomed houses in districts which, to say the least, are not particularly high class. That is, they are being built among other houses which have been up for many years, and are more or less inferior so far as the type of construction is concerned. That is what the government is doing for these people. And when I say this-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The government is not doing it. The government have not built houses in Toronto.
Mr. MeMASTER: Well, the government takes a great deal of credit for building 77,000 of them. Perhaps they did not do it. I do not know. They did not do it all, because private enterprise is still doing-its part. But it is doing that part, despite the difficulties

National Homing Act
which have been made by the government of Canada in allowing this other building to go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Tory mentality is beyond me!

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that if materials were scarce at any time, and those materials are used up for something else, they are bound to be more scarce? The result is that labour was used up, in the building trades. Prices have gone up to such an extent that, while the builders themselves may have high wages, temporarily, a considerable portion of that goes back to the government by way of taxation. They will suffer from the results of a depression which will come, just the same as any other persons in the community. Everyone will suffer-not only those who cause them, but those who will be the unwitting victims.
I have referred to this accelerated depreciation. I did not intend to go into that tonight. It was just a statement of fact. However, perhaps we should examine it and see what is the result. We see that $1,400,000,000 of accelerated depreciation was given to people who have factories and other commercial building enterprises, for the purpose of helping them to build1. That may not be all they spent; I do not suppose it is. But that $1,400,000,000 would build 175,000 houses at $8,000 each. And you ought to build a pretty fair six-room house for $8,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Whose money is that accelerated depreciation? It is not government money.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is what I am thinking about. I do not care; they have to get it from the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You cannot spend money you never had.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The government could have had it right in their mitt, if they had wanted it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: How?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: By collecting it, the same as they collected on incomes from me and from other people.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: To my knowledge we are collecting it just as fast, if it is accelerated.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not catch the minister's interruption. I could not get what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Make your speech.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
No. When I got to my feet I said I was going to speak for only a
few moments. I wanted to give the minister some help.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: You would not let me choose where I think I could get help, would you?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I could not catch what the minister said, but I think I have the answer. Apparently the minister, who is a great man for undertaking great work, is going to persist in his bad ways and will not take the advice of others who perhaps know something about this problem, so we shall have to let him go ahead and do the best he can. But I suggest that something should be done as quickly as possible to relieve the situation which does exist in Toronto, and it is true of every other city. I can say to the minister I did not think the situation would last this long. I thought that, through the inevitable results of death and people moving, the situation would be relieved, but it has not been relieved to any extent. It is not quite as bad as it was, but it is still bad and I hope the minister will do his best to relieve it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the minister is upset, but I can assure him that he is not half as upset as people who have bought houses and cannot get into them. Pick up the paper any morning and read the cases that have come into court of people who have suffered nervous breakdowns and developed other conditions of bad health as a result of not being able to get into the houses they have purchased in good faith. I think rental regulations are absolutely imperative. We cannot permit people to start wholesale moving, even if they have bought houses. It would merely add to the confusion and congestion.
I have in my hand a page from a Winnipeg newspaper which is undertaking to inform the public as to the actual conditions under which people are forced to live. It is not only the person on a low income or without wages who is now finding himself in this terrible and distressing position, but there just are not enough living units for our population, and while I think the immigration policy of the government is perfectly justified-no one will say that we could not use immigrants and no one will say that we have not the responsibility to take immigrants-yet no one can deny that by admitting immigrants we are just adding to the demand for more housing and our situation will thereby become much worse instead of better.
I have in this paper pictures of families huddled in one room, under the most trying sort of family arrangements. If the minister
National Housing Act

would only set up housekeeping and try to live with three or four people in one room, do the dishes, dry the baby's laundry, and try to look after the children doing their homework, with someone in the household perhaps working on a night shift, he would know what these conditions mean to family life. It is a wonder that there are not more families breaking up and more mothers in mental hospitals and more fathers running away and deserting their families. I do not wonder that fathers leave home and mothers go crazy under such conditions. I am surprised that there are not more cases of that kind when one considers the strain we put on human beings by forcing them to accept this sort of living conditions.
I am holding in my hand a picture of one family. Their residence consists of one room, measuring nine by twelve feet. Five persons-a couple and their three children- live in that one room. The father, who was evicted from another home two months ago, has been searching for a suite since he first brought his family to this room, but cannot find anything within his ability to pay, which is $25.
The three children in this family, aged six, four and two, use the muddy, junk-strewn, half-lane shown in the photo as a playground. Beyond it is a busy street screaming with continuous traffic. That single door is the entrance to their room where the two-year old youngster, on account of lack of room, must sleep in a baby carriage. Three administrations-civic, provincial and federal-have faced the problem of Winnipeg's shocking housing conditions, but the problem still remains unsolved.
The newspaper goes on to point out that there are places where there are empty houses, but they are not being used because the cost of occupancy is beyond the means of the people who should be occupying a home.
I want to suggest to the minister that, although many thousands of homes have been built under various schemes, there is no use in considering this housing situation as a temporary emergency. Old and well-developed democracies like Great Britain, the United States and Sweden, and any civilized country that attempts to care for the needs of its population, have been forced to enter the field of subsidized low-rental housing. There is nothing new about it; there is nothing risky about it; there is no debate about it. Every country with any regard for human decency undertakes it as a permanent feature of modern civilization. It is as simple and basic as that, and it is time we accepted that as a principle

and quit thinking in terms merely of the financial angle of it, as we do at present.
The National Housing Act has built many houses and will build many more, but it is designed to give the greatest assistance to those who need it the least. It is designed to make a very profitable investment outlet for the life insurance companies, which get five per cent on their money with no risk. It is a life insurance housing scheme which is completely beyond the reach of the people who need it most, the people who are living under the conditions described and pictured in this paper. I should like to send it over to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Are you sure it is safe for me to read it?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What has that- to do with wages in 1948?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
What has the cost of living to do with it? The cost of living today far more than cancels out any gain in wages.
I think most people agree with me. They are not on cabinet ministers' salaries, and they are trying to live within their incomes. According to the Canada Year Book for 1947, approximately 80 per cent of the total labour force made less than $2,000 in 1946. Our own figures indicate that at least a third of our people will never be able to own their own homes because they have large families and small incomes. I wish to point out to the minister that it is the people with small incomes who have the large families. It has always been so.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Is that so?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, and the minister only needs to look at his own figures.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not agree.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not going to argue biology with the minister, but I am suggesting what the statistics seem to indicate. We find that some countries have undertaken to meet the needs of these families. For instance, we find that Sweden has undertaken to reduce the rent as the family goes up. That is a very useful and sensible thing to do and it should be supported. Under the Swedish housing plan, we find that a family with one child receives a 10 per cent rebate from the city; a family with two children receives a 20 per cent rebate, and so on up to as high as 70 per cent, on the initial rent. Thus, a family with three children would pay $250 rent a year for a smart three-roomed flat with kitchen and bath, instead of $360, while a family with five children would pay only $180 for the same flat.
I do not think the private home owner can afford to subsidize children. Canada is investing quite considerable sums in her children. The biggest payment in our social security
expenditure is our family allowances, and I think it is the soundest expenditure made. This year it will cost us $267 million to help to see that our children get such things as milk, oranges and shoes. If we are to spend $267 million on family allowances we should spend something on subsidized housing to make sure that these families have enough sleeping accommodation, a decent area in which to play, planned residential areas where there are parks and playgrounds and where traffic does not come. We have to begin to plan for people in this country instead of planning for life insurance and investment companies. Our utter contempt of human beings is abominable, and it is time that we began to see the human factor in this housing need, and arrange our finances accordingly.
There is not much more that I want to say, except to repeat that every civilized country in the world is doing something about a permanent long-term plan for subsidized low-rental housing. I have seen them in Washington; I have seen them around New York;
I have seen them in many places. New Zealand has done wonderful work. I saw their houses. They imported Canadian lumber to build them. We have not an excuse in this country. The fact that after the war we began to build cocktail bars, bowling alleys and theatres is a reflection-

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The government?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
We permitted these people to go into that kind of thing. The government did it. These things absorbed our building supplies, and I do not think we should ever have denied the children of this country and permitted these people to build these luxury and unnecessary things which could have waited. The families of this country should come first. When you see that New York is going to pour $325 million into housing in three categories, not only subsidized housing but other kinds as well, it makes you stop and think. New York is going into non-subsidized housing, paying economic rent, because they see that there are people who can afford to pay rent but are not getting places because private enterprise cannot begin to meet the needs of construction.
In the March 22 issue of the Christian Science Monitor an excellent survey of New York's plans appears. It covers veterans housing, non-subsidized housing and subsidized housing for the low-rental group. Therefore I would urge the minister to bring Canada back to the level of other civilized countries and as a permanent plan, to embark on a provision for this kind of assistance to people who
National Housing Act

will not otherwise be housed decently. Surely we have some responsibility to see that every Canadian has a good home and a good environment in which to raise healthy children.

In fairness I must say that I refer to the hardworking gentleman representing Bow River (Mr. Johnston). There is one thing that I do not like to see continuing, and that is the rise in the cost of housing. While the opposition has been steadily pounding at the continued rise in the cost of housing, no solution has yet been proposed. We all know that in 1939 we could build a house for approximately half what we have to pay today. I built a twelve-roomed house in 1943 and it cost me S5,900. Anyone who wishes to see a picture of it can come up to my room and I will show him one. It is all stuccoed, has electric lights and every convenience. Since that time, labour costs have risen from sixty cents an hour to $1.60.

National Housing Act
In Windsor at the present time carpenters are on strike holding up construction; bricklayers were on strike a while ago holding up construction; electricians have been on strike holding up construction. They will not work for less than $1.65 an hour and they do not do half a day's work compared with what they used to do.
The ordinary man who wants to have a plumbing job done for $5 or $10 cannot get an ordinary plumber but a man who has joined a union and who is paid $2 an hour for fiddling around the pipe. By the time he gets the job done his bill is approximately $50. I do not care what anyone says; I will say here and now that labour has to be told when the end is reached. When a man works eight hours a day and gets $20 he is not getting what should be coming to him. The people who work in order to provide food for the nation, producing it from the sea and the land, have to work also. People must be told that if they are to survive they have to work for what they get.
We have been debating freight rates at considerable length in this house. I am off the subject at the moment, but as soon as things are ironed out and there is enough money so that the railways can balance things, there is another threatened strike for a 25 per cent or 30 per cent increase. I know there was a time when I worked for thirty cents an hour and got $2.40 a day. Now they are asking for an increase of thirty cents an hour all at once. These things have to stop, or we shall have a serious depression and labour will be the first to suffer.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Are you speaking for the government?

speechtext:
As I said before, the cost of housing is too high for the average man; unless we can find some way of building a house for the average man, it will cost between $4,000 and $5,000, and in my honest opinion he will never be able to pay for it. But there are many people who are looking for high-class houses and are driving $2,000 automobiles. The luxuries come first.
We might as well face the facts right now. We have to cut our coat according to our cloth, and if there were more people who had that frame of mind the situation would be greatly relieved.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? After his disparaging remarks about labour unions, does he remember when he and I were taking $1 a hundred for milk and formed a milk producers' association to enable us to get a better price for our
