speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall not be long. I would judge from the remarks which have been made that Canada is doing very little in housing. It has been pointed out that we have a report, the Curtis report, made in 1943, and it has been quoted by every member who has risen to speak. The problem of Canada was to build 750,000 houses in the first ten years after the war. That is the Curtis report. The war ended on September 1, 1945, and it is now 1948, about two and a half years having elapsed. In the two and a half years we have completed well over 200,000 houses. In fact, we are moving at an accelerated rate, and it should be well over 450,000 houses at the end of five years. By the end of ten years it should be at least 1,000,000
National Housing Act

houses, so that we are building at a rate which should be satisfactory according to the Curtis report.
Anyone familiar with statistics knows that Canada has completed, since the end of the war, more houses per capita than any other country in the world. You have only to read tonight's paper in which you will find that the vice-president of Queen's university, speaking in Ottawa last night to the mortgage association, made the statement that Canada had built more houses per capita than any country in the world since the war.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Per capita?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. People like to talk about distant places. Well, it so happens that I have the report on New Zealand's housing before and since the war, and it makes the statement that New Zealand, since the war, has built fifty-three houses per 10,000 of population, while in Canada we have built seventy-five houses per 10,000.
There is one point I wish to make. Everyone talks about the need of ho'uses for Canada and talks about subsidized housing as a means of getting these houses built. May I point out that the two questions are absolutely different. The need of Canada at the moment is for roofs over families. That is, the need is for houses; and houses are being built as rapidly as they can be built. It has been suggested here that the government is being niggardly in the matter. The government have not failed to build any houses because the money has not been available. Last year the government built practically every house that every city in Canada would ask us or permit us to build. We were sorry that we could not carry out the program which we planned last year because we could not persuade cities to make the lands available for us to build. This year we have built every house that any city would permit us to build. As I stated, we wanted to build
12,000	houses. At the rate we are going, in closing off the program at June 1 as has been our custom, we shall not succeed in having 12.000 started for the reason that people will not invite us to build houses.
As far as mortgage money is concerned, there has been no limit on it. Any one who wants to borrow under the National Housing Act is free to do so. There is no limitation there. I just want to point out that fact, because everyone who gets up says that the government is being niggard!}7, that it is stingy about this and stingy about that.
What about subsidized housing? Subsidized housing does not build one more house, and

it would not build one more house. It would just change the economic level of the people who occupy the houses that are built. Every house that is built is occupied. My hon. friend has stated that in Winnipeg there are houses which are unoccupied. I venture to say that there are no more than one week's construction of houses that are unoccupied in Winnipeg. We are constantly getting demands from there for more houses, and we are building more houses. I was out there last summer when we had 2,300 houses under construction in Winnipeg. It was an eye-opener to me to see how many houses 2,300 actually are. I went up one street and down another for all of one day to see the construction that Wartime Housing was doing in that city.
The point is this. Canada needs houses. These houses are occupied by people who are able to pay the rent. I say that because they are paying the rent. The arrears in rent in all Canada are less than one week's rent; there are practically no arrears in rent in all Canada. There may be people who cannot pay the minimum rent. But those people are under cover and I think it will be agreed that, as long as people who are able to pay economic rent cannot get houses, they are the first people entitled to obtain them.
The day may come when subsidizing rentals or subsidizing houses may enable houses to be found by people who do not have them today. But that is not today. It is absolute nonsense to talk about Canada's housing problem being due to lack of subsidization. It has nothing at all to do with the number of houses being built. I simply want to make that point. Since I am speaking by unanimous consent, I should not speak too long.
Having made the first point, I will make my other remarks in committee. Before sitting down, I should like to make a few remarks about the speech delivered by the hon. member for High Park (Mr. McMaster). I dare say he is an eminent lawyer, and I claim some little fame in building. But I must say that if he knows anything about building, I will admit that I know nothing about law. However, Mr. Speaker, I will finish my remarks in committee.
Motion (Mr. Howe) agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I did not speak in the debate on the motion to go into committee, Mr. Chairman, and I do not intend to speak now. I want to ask the minister just one question. I have always been under the impression that some sort of subsidization plan would help the people of Canada in a house

National Housing Act
building program, particularly those in the lower income brackets. I am not overly critical of what the government have tried to do with respect to housing. When I go into various cities and find the vast building program that has been going on over the years, I am quite confident that something at least has been done. But that does not render the situation any less important when there is still a housing crisis.
As I see it, the picture is that the people in the lower income brackets apparently cannot afford to build under present conditions. That is a serious matter. A person with a fair income, provided that he can scrape together $1,000 or $2,000, after passing or complying with all sorts of rules and regulations, eventually may be able to purchase on some long-term payment plan. But all people are not in the fair-size income brackets. Some people are in the small income brackets, and when it comes to renting any place today they are required to pay a larger rent than I believe they can afford with their incomes. The question I want to ask is this. The minister has just said that a subsidization plan would not help the housing situation today. Does he mean to say that if there were a subsidization plan, no more houses would be built than are being built today? Is that what he means to say?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, that is exactly what I mean to say. I may say that the province of Ontario have started a subsidization plan. They are willing to pay up to $1,200 a house after the government gets through lending money. I venture the opinion that the plan will not put one additional roof over one additional family in this countiy over the next year or two.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: To me that does not seem to be reasonable. What reason has the minister to believe that? If there were a subsidization plan, it simply means that money would be available in larger quantities than it is today. Or if you want to put it in another way, if there were a subsidization plan, the cost of building would be reduced. It must help somewhere if there is a subsidization plan. What reason is there, then, for saying that there would not be more building than there is now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: May I answer that by saying that the reason is that houses at any prices sell today. They all sell. The fact that they sell for $4,000 instead of $8,000 would not build any more houses. All houses that can be built today can be sold for their economic price,

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Even that does not make it plain to me. It may be plain to the minister. but not to me. Suppose I wanted to build
a house and I was able to get money through some sort of subsidization plan, it seems to me I would likely start building, if I could not get a house any other way. That would be another house being built; and if several thousand people were in a similar financial position, then it would amount to several thousand homes. It seems to me that the answer must be that either material or labour is not available, or perhaps both; and if that is the case that may be the answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: It is the answer.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
But in that case my suggestion would be that it must be somebody's responsibility to see that the production of building material is speeded up; and I do not think anyone is more capable of seeing to that than the government in power. That is my way of looking at the situation.
There is another matter in connection with low-rental housing. Has the government considered at all the building of small apartment blocks for the housing of perhaps four to eight families at really low rentals? When I say "low rentals" I do not mean $40 or $50. I think the figure of $38 was mentioned the other day. I do not call $38 a low rental. I call a low rental something like $18 or $20 or $25, which is about as much as the average wage earner can afford to pay. Has the government considered that? It seems to me that such apartments, not cheaply built but perhaps frame structures, or of the stucco type-not of brick and with a lot of fancy things that are unnecessary-built at reasonable cost to house four to eight families, with the same heating unit for all, could be rented at reasonable rates. I am not a businessman, and I am speaking only from my own common sense in the matter, but has the government considered anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend is describing a popular type of rental unit in Montreal, which is the cold-water flat. It is a building with from four to eight apartments, built at as low a cost as apartments can be built; but the rentals for those apartments are not in the range mentioned by my hon. friend. The cheapest unit than can be built is the five-room bungalow, and that is the popular house today.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: What does that rent for?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.

speechtext:
The first provision of this resolution authorizes approved lending institutions to purchase from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages held by
National Housing Act

that corporation. How did the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation acquire those mortgages, and what is the reason for selling them?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, the central mortgage
corporation has been selling wartime houses, taking a down payment and a mortgage and giving title to the house. It holds those mortgages, and we are now being authorized to sell them to the insurance companies if it seems wise to do so at any stage. We have not that power today.
In this connection I want to say just one thing. Everybody is sneering at the insurance companies and saying we are protecting them. What is an insurance company? It represents the savings of the Canadian people. This is not some great corporation that is making huge profits out of this business; it is a company that is looking after your savings and mine. I hope there is not a man in this house who has not life insurance. W'hen we say we are protecting the insurance companies, we are protecting the savings of the Canadian people invested in life insurance, the greatest pool of investment money in this country. My C.C.F. friends can sneer at people who buy insurance and try to protect their old age, but I offer this house no apology for sponsoring legislation that will prevent the insurance funds of this country from being lost in a government housing venture.
Mr. MaeINNIS: I object to the minister referring to the C.C.F. as sneering at this. I am not sneering at the minister or at anything he does.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I realize that. I was referring to other speeches.
Mr. MaeINNIS: The minister says the insurance companies are using his money and mine. Well, the government is collecting my money and his, and if a profit can be made out of these mortgages-and I cannot see the insurance companies buying them if a profit cannot be made-there is no reason why the government should not act in that capacity and save that amount of taxation. The question I asked is perfectly reasonable. Now the government has to go into the housing business to guarantee, by this measure, the money the insurance companies invest in housing. If the government itself is investing in housing at a profitable rate, why should the government have to sell these mortgages to the insurance companies?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
So that the money recovered from the mortgages can be used to build more houses.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Can it not be used to build more houses if the government has the mortgages? Cannot the government handle a revolving housing fund just as an insurance company does?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Not if it keeps the money frozen in mortgages.
Mr. MaeINNIS: The insurance companies are not building houses. The only effective low-rental housing is that which has been built by the government itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, but I am pointing out to my hon. friend that the government may wish to build houses, that it may want to use the money recovered from the sale of those houses to build still more. It cannot do so if all that money is tied up in mortgages. You cannot spend a mortgage in building a house. We are only taking power to do this in the event that we may want liquid funds. To have a revolving fund we must keep it liquid; and the only way we can keep the fund liquid is to sell the mortgages.
Mr. MaeINNIS: My hon. friend cannot have it both ways. If the insurance companies buy these mortgages they wrill not have the funds to invest in further house building, any more than the government would. I am using the minister's own argument now. The argument the minister has presented is not sensible, and is not the kind I think he can put up if he wishes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is perfectly logical. Suppose the government has $500 million invested in houses, and it sells perhaps $50,000,000 worth. It would like to replace those houses it has sold by building another $50,000,000 worth of houses. You may say it has $50,000,000 because it has just sold houses worth that much, but it has not that money in a spendable form. It has an investment in mortgages for the most part. The insurance companies have free money because they have premium income which requires to be invested. You cannot invest money and spend it too.
Mr. MaeINNIS: Is the government going to build more houses with the money it will get from the sale of these mortgages?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply

The minister cannot expect us to accept that sort of explanation. During the war, when emergency housing was needed, the government did not have to go to the insurance companies to get the necessary capital to build wartime housing. The job was done without that. The minister should give us some more sensible explanation as to why this time it is proposed to turn the job over to the insurance companies. The other day the minister's speech indicated that the relationship with Housing Enterprises, a subsidiary of the insurance companies, was quite unsatisfactory. For him now to propose, as this resolution sets out-
... to authorize approved lending institutions to purchase from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation mortgages held by the said corporation and to make loans to owners of rental housing . . .
-is not a satisfactory explanation. He should indicate what the plans are. Does the government propose to reinvest in additional wartime housing, if certain securities are sold to the insurance companies?

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.

If the minister does not wish to answer at this stage, possibly tomorrow he can give us the information. I would ask him to explain the difference between rental insurance and subsidized housing. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard referred to a speech made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs some time ago, in which the minister said, "No government of which I form a part will ever pass legislation for subsidized housing."
It would appear to me that, while this is not. called subsidized housing, it is doing the thing which the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that no government of which he formed a part would do. The only difference is that this is guaranteeing that certain lending institutions will have a fixed income which will cover taxes, services, operating expenses, repairs, renewals, replacements, and a reasonable return on investments.
According to this, public funds will be taken from the consolidated revenue fund of our country to subsidize one group. Would the minister explain to the committee the difference between rental insurance and subsidized housing?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Rental insurance is like any other insurance in that a fund is set up. It will be understood that this rental insurance is not given free. The government charges a rate which it believes, on the average, will keep the fund solvent. However, the consolidated revenue fund is behind that insurance fund. If a terrible depression were to come upon us, such as my hon. friend loves to predict, and has done, ever since the war, the fund might become insolvent, and the revenue fund would have to get behind it. On the other hand, we might keep a Liberal government in power for a long time, and have prosperous times, in which event the fund would make a great deal of money.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO POWERS OF APPROVED LENDING INSTITUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I do not think a depression is necessary. But I would remind the minister that in 1945 he brought in a white paper anticipating that a depression would come, and outlining the course Canada should follow.

I do not wish to see the resolution passed this evening, because there are other questions I should like to ask.
National Housing Act

Coming from a riding such as Rosedale, in the city of Toronto, where the Regent Park development is taking place, I believe the minister will be well aware of conditions in certain sections of my constituency. May I point out to him that, while he said a short time ago that if we had subsidization or some other form of government assistance there would not be any more houses built, I do not think that statement is fully warranted from all aspects.
I would point out to the committee that, while in Toronto there is not much land available for large-scale developments, there is plenty of land for apartment houses and the building of duplexes. A year ago the total amount of construction which went into housing development was 15 per cent. The report of the building commissioner of that city was made available recently. That report is for last year, and it shows that the amount of building construction in 1947 which went into the construction of houses was 6-6 per cent. The reason for that is that the other 93-4 per cent went into commercial and industrial construction-moving picture palaces, of which there were a considerable number, warehouses, branches of factories and additions to various other forms of construction where a profit could be obtained.
The reason that type of development is not restrained in any way is that the cost of construction of a property for business purposes is a relatively small element in the affairs of the business. On the other hand, when a man builds a house it involves a very large
portion of his total budget. He cannot afford the high material costs and high wage rates which go into the building.
I suggest to the minister that if we had had some form of control-and it would have to be in this instance some form of federal control, because the municipalities were competing with each other in the matter of building -we would have had more houses available for veterans and other people who are in dire need at the present time.
For that reason I suggest to the minister that his department and the government have not carried out the housing program as they should have. There should have been some form of direction of these matters, so that more houses could have been built-not necessarily within the political confines of a ci1y like Toronto, but in the suburbs around the city where a limited amount of housing construction is going on.
